Glossary
Term Description
Application Component A deployable, modular piece of software that provides a
defined set of functionality and holds the data it manages,
exposing both through services.
Application Service An explicitly defined unit of application behaviour. An
application service exposes the functionality of an application
component to its environment.
Capability A high-level ability the health system possesses or needs in
order to achieve its goals. It expresses what the health system
is able to do, independently of how that ability is implemented.
Business Domain A specific focus area or subsystem within a broader business
system, characterized by its own essential attributes [Under
review]
Outcome An end result or consequence of a set of activities; an outcome
is often measurable and signals progress towards a goal.
Product A concrete offering, bundling services and data, that is made
available to stakeholders.
Business Services layer A layer of the reference architecture grouping the health
capabilities that national health systems strive to deliver across
their principal domains — clinical care, public health, the health
supply chain, and health financing — together with the shared
components that enable them.
Client Members of the public who are potential or current users of
health services, including health prevention and wellness
activities.
Data Governance The structures and standards (policies & legal frameworks)
necessary to coordinate and manage the data journey from
collection, storage, sharing, analysis to use to produce trusted,
secure and quality data for decision making
Data Object A defined unit of structured data used or produced by an
application component.
Digital Health The systematic application of information and communications
technologies, computer science, and data to support informed
decision-making by individuals, the health workforce, and
health systems, to strengthen resilience to disease and
improve health and wellness.
Digital Infrastructure Infrastructures in the digital domain are digital resources, such
as systems and specifications, built as shared means to
achieve many ends
Digital Public Infrastructure A set of shared digital systems that should be secure and
(DPI) interoperable, and can be built on open standards and
specifications to deliver and provide equitable access to public
and/or private services at societal scale and are governed by
applicable legal frameworks and enabling rules to drive
development, inclusion, innovation, trust, and competition,
while respecting human rights and fundamental freedoms.
(G20/UNDP)
Enterprise Architecture The organising logic for business processes and IT
infrastructure reflecting the integration and
standardisation requirements of the organisation's operating
model. [Under review]
Fast Healthcare FHIR is a standard for healthcare data exchange, published by
Interoperability Resources HL7®
(FHIR)
Functional application Functional applications are application components that deliver
a specific operational function within a defined domain. They
are context-specific, reflecting the operational requirements of
a programme, scheme, or institution that procures them.
Goal A high-level statement of intent, direction, or desired state for
an organisation and its stakeholders.
Health Digital Public Health Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI-H) refers to digital
Infrastructure resources that are built as a shared means for fulfilling multiple
health agency functions.
Health Information [To be included before publication]
Exchange
Health Programme Health programmes are structured and coordinated
interventions and services, delivered to defined populations or
patient groups, to prevent disease, promote health, and
address specific health needs.
Integration Bespoke capability of connecting one application component to
another [Under review]
Interoperability Interoperability is the standards-based capability of
heterogeneous information systems to communicate,
exchange data, and use the exchanged information to execute
functions effectively.
Logical Observation LOINC is a common language (a set of identifiers, names, and
Identifiers Names and codes) for identifying health measurements, observations, and
Codes documents.
(LOINC)
Point-of-service applications Point-of-service applications are end-user application
components (IT systems or software tools) used by individuals
directly engaged in healthcare—such as clinicians, community
health workers, and patients—that enable interaction with the
broader healthcare ecosystem. [Under review]
Reference Architecture A technology-neutral blueprint that captures the common
building blocks, relationships, and design principles of a
technical environment.
Registry A governed, authoritative and centralized information system
that captures, stores and maintains the unique attributes and
identifiers of health facilities, health service users, health
products and/or the health workforce using a predefined
canonical minimum data set. [Under review]
Repository
SMART Guidelines Standards-based, Machine-readable, Adaptive,
Requirements-based, Testable Guidelines are a
comprehensive set of reusable digital health components (e.g.,
interoperability standards, code libraries, algorithms, technical
and operational specifications) that transform the guideline
adaptation and implementation process to preserve fidelity and
accelerate uptake. SMART Guidelines provide a five-step
pathway to advance the adoption of best clinical and data
practices, even if a country is not yet fully digital.
SNOMED CT Systematized Nomenclature of Medicine Clinical Terms is a
structured clinical terminology standard for use in electronic
health records.
SNOMED GPS Systematized Nomenclature of Medicine – Global Patient Set
is a list of basic clinical terms. It is an open and freely
accessible subset of SNOMED CT terms that represents the
breadth of concepts included in the SNOMED CT International
Edition.
Solution Architecture The design of a specific application component or HDPI
expressed through specifications and diagrams [Under review]
Stakeholder An individual, role, or organisation with an interest in the
outcomes of the architecture.
Value The benefit or utility a stakeholder gains from using a service,
product, or capability.

lines.2: Countries are unlikely to achieve their health goals through investing in isolated or siloed health
lines.3: systems. Instead, they should build shared data and digital capabilities that support multiple
lines.4: programmes, multiple diseases and multiple levels of care.
lines.5: This Reference Architecture Guidance for Digital Public Infrastructure for Health (DPI-H) sets
lines.6: out how countries can build those shared foundations. It is written for the governments,
lines.7: development partners and technical stakeholders responsible for planning, financing and
lines.8: implementing national digital health infrastructure, and it brings policy intent and technical
lines.9: design into a single, coherent frame. DPI-H refers to digital resources built as a shared means
lines.10: for fulfilling multiple health agency functions — distinct from the foundational digital public
lines.11: infrastructure, such as identity, payments and data exchange, upon which the health sector can
lines.12: build.
lines.13: There is a need for solid foundations based on common structures and standards, that are
lines.14: applicable and adaptable to local contexts, to strengthen data and digital infrastructure and
lines.15: architecture. These foundations should promote:
lines.16: a) The production of trusted, secure and quality data for decision making,
lines.17: b) Interoperability as a cross-cutting property of the architecture, and
lines.18: c) The grounding of health digital public infrastructure (DPI-H) in common standards.
lines.19: In turn these are essential foundations for ‘AI for health’ and ‘AI-ready data’.
lines.20: The Reference Architecture Guidance also recognises the complex state of digital
lines.21: implementations across countries and proposes adaptive architecture concepts to suit different
lines.22: contexts, and which can be achievable by countries. It recognises resource constraints in low-
lines.23: and middle-income countries, that a one-size-fits-all approach is not realistic, and acknowledges
lines.24: varying starting points for countries, providing implementation pathways suited to each context.
lines.25: The guidance also introduces the concept of Resilient Essential Data and Digital Health
lines.26: Infrastructure (REDDHI) — the state that countries are working towards through their digital
lines.27: health investments — and describes the minimum set of shared capabilities and application
lines.28: components that form the foundation of REDDHI. This provides countries with a practical entry
lines.29: point for their DPI-H journey, whatever their current context.
lines.30: To connect these foundations to concrete outcomes, the guidance takes an enterprise
lines.31: architecture approach, using the established TOGAF® and ArchiMate® methods, anchored on
lines.32: seven priority health goals: building trusted data foundations; supporting a capable, well-
lines.33: distributed health workforce; ensuring quality and continuity of care; establishing trusted
lines.34: personal health records; optimising supply chain management; strengthening health financing;
lines.35: and building resilience to climate change and epidemics. Each goal is mapped systematically to
lines.36: the shared capabilities and application components required to achieve it, so that architectural

lines.37: choices trace back to the health outcomes they serve rather than being made component by
lines.39: It is important to note that the WHO-ITU DHP Handbook, the OpenHIE Architecture and the
lines.40: DPI-H Reference Architecture recognise similar foundational components such as metadata
lines.41: registries, a terminology services component and interoperability. Accordingly, the guidance
lines.42: builds on proven concepts rather than reinventing them, maintaining continuity with established
lines.43: approaches. However, the Reference Architecture Guidance introduces additional components
lines.44: as DPI-H, reflecting the evolution of technology and learnings from the intervening years.
lines.45: The Reference Architecture Guidance also extends the WHO Digital Implementation Investment
lines.46: Guide (DIIG) by providing the technical and architectural foundation for implementing a national
lines.47: digital health enterprise architecture. The reference architecture specifies the what and how of
lines.48: the enterprise architecture itself, addressing the technical questions that arise during
lines.49: implementation: which types of systems should countries invest in? How do these systems
lines.50: connect and exchange data? What are the dependencies between components? What technical
lines.51: specifications ensure interoperability? Countries using the DIIG to plan their digital health
lines.52: investments can leverage this reference architecture to ensure their technical implementations
lines.53: are coherent, avoid fragmentation, and align with global standards. With both resources,
lines.54: countries can move from strategic intent to technical implementation with confidence that their
lines.55: architectural choices support long-term health sector goals.

lines.61: describes how interoperability is realised as a cross-cutting property of the architecture rather

lines.63: meaning of data over time; and how countries can approach conformance, coverage and
lines.64: progress, the roles and skills required, and the financing and partnership arrangements that
lines.65: make DPI-H sustainable. A dedicated treatment of emerging technologies positions artificial
lines.66: intelligence as a cross-cutting consideration that depends on — and raises the importance of —
lines.67: the trusted, well-governed data foundations the architecture establishes.
lines.68: This guidance was developed jointly by the World Health Organization and the International
lines.69: Telecommunication Union, working with a technical working group drawn from enterprise
lines.70: architecture, clinical, health informatics, public health and digital health backgrounds across
lines.71: low-, middle- and high-income settings. It applies established enterprise architecture methods
lines.72: — TOGAF® and ArchiMate® — and builds on existing frameworks, including the OpenHIE
lines.73: Architecture, the WHO-ITU Digital Health Platform Handbook and the WHO Digital
lines.74: Implementation Investment Guide. It was refined through successive rounds of drafting and
lines.75: expert review and released for public consultation ahead of publication.

lines.9: health architectures using enterprise architecture approaches, but guidance at the level of
lines.10: specificity countries need has not, until now, been widely available. This guidance responds to

lines.62: Two dimensions of this definition warrant particular attention. The first is the emphasis on
lines.63: shared means. DPI-H is not a collection of programme-specific tools or point-of-service
lines.64: applications; it is infrastructure that is shared, reusable, and available to all actors within the
lines.65: health system without requiring each to build equivalent capabilities independently. The second
lines.66: is the relationship between DPI-H and foundational DPI. DPI-H does not seek to replicate what
lines.67: foundational DPI provides; rather, it extends and complements them with the domain-specific
lines.68: capabilities that the health sector requires but that general-purpose DPI cannot accommodate.
lines.69: Where foundational DPI exists and is accessible, DPI-H builds upon it. Where it does not, DPI-H
lines.70: provides the essential capabilities the health system needs to function while remaining
lines.71: architecturally open to integration as the broader digital ecosystem matures.
lines.72: Together, these two dimensions — shared infrastructure and purposeful extension of
lines.73: foundational DPI — define what distinguishes DPI-H from the vertical, programme-driven
lines.74: systems, functional applications, and point-of-service solutions that have historically
lines.75: characterised health sector digitalisation. Where those approaches have delivered value within
lines.76: their individual contexts, they have done so at the cost of fragmentation, duplication, and limited
lines.77: interoperability across the health system as a whole. DPI-H establishes a different foundation:
lines.78: shared, reusable, and governed infrastructure upon which programmes, applications, and
lines.79: services can be built to fulfil multiple health agency functions, without recreating the capabilities
lines.80: that should be common to all. It is this architectural logic that underpins the reference
lines.81: architecture presented in this guidance document.
lines.83: The DPI-H reference architecture guidance builds substantively upon and extends the
lines.84: foundational work of the 2020 WHO-ITU Digital Health Platform (DHP) Handbook and the
lines.85: OpenHIE Architecture Specification and draws on standard architectural guidance from The
lines.87: The reference architecture guidance addresses the maturation of national digital ecosystems
lines.88: where health is one sector leveraging common DPI rather than building parallel systems

lines.172: 1.2 Why health needs more than foundational DPI
lines.174: A recurring theme in digital public infrastructure discourse is that sectors should leverage
lines.175: foundational DPIs — identity, payments, and data exchange — rather than build parallel,
lines.176: sector-specific equivalents that reinforce fragmentation of a country’s digital architecture. This is
lines.177: sound guidance where foundational DPIs exist, are trustworthy, and are accessible, and the
lines.178: health sector should build on them wherever it can. Foundational DPIs are, by design, general-
lines.179: purpose: they provide broadly reusable capabilities and deliberately leave sector-specific logic
lines.180: to the sectors that use them. Health, however, presents conditions that require more than
lines.181: foundational DPI can currently provide — in some cases because foundational DPI is genuinely
lines.182: absent or incomplete, and in others because the capability belongs with health-specific
lines.183: components by design. The aim is not to create permanent parallel infrastructure, but to
lines.184: leverage foundational DPI where it serves, add health-specific components where it does not,
lines.185: and ensure that gaps in foundational DPI do not become a barrier to delivering care.
lines.187: For a significant number of low- and middle-income countries, foundational DPIs are either
lines.188: nascent or absent. This means that in some cases, even where a country has foundational
lines.189: DPIs, health may require specific capabilities, exchange standards, and governance
lines.190: arrangements that go beyond what a general-purpose DPI can provide. Where foundational
lines.191: DPIs do not yet exist — as is the case in many low- and middle-income countries — health
lines.192: systems cannot wait. Care delivery, disease surveillance, health financing and supply chain
lines.193: management need to function in the present.
lines.195: 1.2.1 Identity DPI and Identification in Healthcare
lines.197: Consider identity. A national ID system establishes who a person is, but health requires knowing
lines.198: what a person is eligible for, what treatments they are receiving, what medications have been
lines.199: dispensed, and whether they have consented to share specific data with specific actors.
lines.200: Foundational identity DPI also has genuine coverage gaps for populations the health sector is
lines.201: obligated to serve; it does not typically cover newborns prior to civil registration, refugees,
lines.202: undocumented migrants, or other marginalised groups. Clinical settings also routinely encounter
lines.203: patients who present without documentation, requiring probabilistic matching, duplicate
lines.204: detection, and family linkage capabilities that are simply outside the scope of general-purpose
lines.205: identity DPI. These represent routine operational requirements in health systems worldwide,
lines.206: rather than edge cases. Box 2 sets out where foundational identity DPI, on its own, does not

unnumbered: Box 1.2: Why foundational identity DPI is not sufficient for health on its own
Foundational digital identity provides authoritative identification and authentication of
individuals. The health requirements below reflect genuine gaps, others reflect capabilities
that belong with health components by design — in both cases, foundational identity is
necessary but not sufficient on its own:
1. Coverage Gaps: Foundational identity systems may not cover vulnerable populations who
need health services—newborns (before civil registration), refugees, undocumented migrants,
and marginalized communities. The health sector is required to provide universal access
regardless of legal identity status. These gaps have downstream consequences: where
individuals are missing from or inconsistently identified in the population base, it becomes
harder to establish reliable denominators for disease surveillance and population health
monitoring, and continuity of care is weakened when a person cannot be consistently
recognised across visits, providers, or over time.
2. Purpose Limitations: National ID proves who you are but not what you're eligible for.
Health services require additional context: health coverage schemes, programme enrollment
(e.g., for HIV treatment, TB medication), service entitlements, and consent status—which are
not provided by foundational identity systems.
3. Privacy and Consent Granularity: Health data demands more stringent privacy
protections and granular consent management than general identity systems typically provide.
Patients may consent to sharing data with their physician but not with researchers, or allow
access to vaccination records but not mental health records—nuances foundational identity
systems don't address.
4. Clinical Matching Requirements: Healthcare requires probabilistic matching algorithms
for patients presenting without identification, duplicate detection across misspelled names or
missing data, and family relationship linkages—capabilities beyond simple identity verification.
5. Multiple Health Identifiers: Health ecosystems often have context-specific identifiers—
patient medical record numbers, health coverage scheme member IDs, clinical trial participant
IDs—that serve different purposes than national identity and these cannot be simply replaced
by a single foundational ID.
6. Cross-Border Care: National identity systems are country-specific, but health services
increasingly require cross-border recognition for migrants, travelers, and regional health
initiatives—a gap foundational identity DPI doesn't inherently solve.
These highlight the need for a health-specific DPI component that bridges foundational
identity (when available) with health-specific requirements. It provides universal coverage
including those without legal ID, manages health-specific attributes and consents, enables
clinical matching algorithms, and maintains health system identifiers while linking to national
ID where it exists. The reference architecture positions Client Registry as the health sector's
identity DPI that integrates with but doesn't depend entirely on foundational DPI identity
systems.

lines.210: 1.2.2 Data exchange DPI and Interoperability in the health sector
lines.212: A similar pattern emerges when examining foundational data exchange DPI. Health systems
lines.213: involve a wide range of actors — ministries, facilities, clinicians, programme managers, health
lines.214: coverage schemes, supply chain operators, researchers, and patients themselves — each with
lines.215: different informational needs that no single system can meet alone. General-purpose data
lines.216: exchange DPI are designed to move data securely between systems, and they are agnostic to
lines.217: the content they carry. This content-neutrality keeps the exchange layer simple, broadly
lines.218: reusable across sectors, and free of any single sector's business logic, while keeping
lines.219: accountability for that business logic with the institutions that own it.
lines.221: However, the health sector has requirements that foundational data exchange, on its own, does
lines.222: not address — both in how data must be understood when it moves and in how far it must
lines.223: travel. Box 3 sets out where foundational data exchange DPI does not, by itself, meet health-
lines.224: sector needs, and the gaps the health sector aims to bridge.

unnumbered: Box 1.3: Why foundational data exchange DPI is not sufficient for health on its own
Foundational data exchange DPI provides secure, authenticated, logged, reliable transport
between registered parties. Like a postal service that delivers a sealed envelope without
opening it, the data exchange DPI carries data between systems without reading or
interpreting its contents. The capabilities below are health-sector requirements essential to
health data exchange that this transport, on its own, does not provide.
1. Structural, semantic, and message-format interoperability: Clinical and health-related
data need to be structurally consistent, semantically unambiguous, and exchanged in
recognised health message formats — such as HL7 FHIR — so that they are interpreted
consistently across systems, including where systems use differing or older formats. General-
purpose data exchange DPI is designed to move data securely (encrypted end to end) but is
agnostic to its structure, meaning, and format, carrying messages between systems without
reading or reconciling their contents.
2. Cross-Border and Multi-Jurisdiction Exchange
Health increasingly requires the exchange of information across borders — for migrants,
travellers, regional disease surveillance, and emergency response. Foundational data
exchange DPI is typically national in scope; cross-border health data exchange depends on
shared information standards, such as the International Patient Summary, and on legal and
governance frameworks for health data that extend beyond any single national data exchange
DPI.

lines.369: The design and implementation of Digital Public Infrastructure for Health is guided by a set of
lines.370: principles that reflect the technical requirements of shared digital infrastructure and the
lines.371: responsibilities inherent in managing health data at population scale. At its foundation, DPI-H
lines.372: promotes the use of open standards and interoperable design, enabling systems to exchange
lines.373: data reliably and evolve without vendor lock-in. The principles below should inform every aspect
lines.374: of how DPI-H is conceived, built, governed, and sustained.
lines.376: Interoperability: DPI-H should support both data and system interoperability, enabling the
lines.377: exchange and use of information across platforms, providers, and potentially, sectors. It is
lines.378: designed to accommodate domain-specific extensions without disrupting other users or
lines.379: systems, ensuring that as the health digital ecosystem grows, continuity and scalability are
lines.382: Reusability: DPI-H components should be designed for reuse across programmes and use
lines.383: cases, allowing shared functionality and data to serve multiple purposes without duplication.
lines.384: This reduces cost, lowers implementation burden, and provides a stable foundation upon which
lines.385: additional solutions — public and private — can be built and iterated.
lines.387: Open Standards and Specifications: DPI-H should be built on open standards, specifications,
lines.388: and APIs developed through recognised Standards Development Organisations (SDOs) and
lines.389: open governance processes that are inclusive in participation and accessible in their outputs.
lines.390: Open standards promote interoperability, portability, and transparency, enable consistent data
lines.391: structures, and support the long-term sustainability of national digital health investments by
lines.394: Public Governance: DPI-H should be governed in the public interest under clear legal and
lines.395: regulatory frameworks that protect privacy, security, and individual rights. Public governance
lines.396: refers to accountable stewardship under public mandate — ensuring the infrastructure fulfils the
lines.397: functions the health sector needs to meet health and health-related needs, and remains subject
lines.398: to institutional oversight — rather than requiring that every component be publicly owned or
lines.399: operated. Components may be built or operated by public, private, or non-governmental actors,
lines.400: provided they remain accountable to public oversight. Such governance structures provide the
lines.401: accountability and trust that are prerequisite to the widespread adoption of shared health
lines.404: Security and Privacy: DPI-H embeds security and privacy protections by design, treating them
lines.405: not as compliance requirements but as foundational architectural properties. Protection
lines.406: encompasses both dimensions — security against unauthorised access, and privacy as a right
lines.407: — ensuring that access to personal health data is controlled, lawful, and appropriate. DPI-H
lines.408: applies zero-trust principles and rights-enhancing measures by default, while also ensuring
lines.409: resilience and continuity of essential health services against evolving cyber and operational

lines.412: Autonomy and Sovereignty: DPI-H supports national ownership and control of digital health
lines.413: systems, enabling countries to implement solutions aligned with their own priorities, policies,
lines.414: and governance structures. Countries should not be dependent on actors outside their
lines.415: jurisdiction for the continued operation or evolution of their core digital health infrastructure, and
lines.416: the capabilities, standards, and governance of DPI-H should remain under national control.
lines.418: These principles establish the foundational character of DPI-H as shared digital infrastructure.
lines.419: The reference architecture that gives effect to these principles is further shaped by a set of
lines.420: architectural principles that govern how DPI-H is designed, structured, and applied in practice —
lines.421: addressed in the Architecture Principles sub-chapter of the Reference Architecture Framework.
lines.423: 1.5 The Seven Priority Health Sector Goals

lines.425: the areas where digital infrastructure can most meaningfully improve health system
lines.426: performance. These goals are not isolated ambitions but mutually reinforcing outcomes that
lines.427: compound in value as the underlying infrastructure matures.

lines.499: and support provider payments can substantially reduce leakage and delay while improving

lines.508: The outcomes these goals describe are not automatic. The extent to which they are realised
lines.509: depends on the quality of implementation and the context in which it takes place; evidence to
lines.510: date shows that benefits anticipated in design are not always borne out in practice. For this

lines.3: The reference architecture for health Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI-H) guidance provides
lines.4: countries with a structured architectural framework for designing national digital health
lines.5: infrastructure that is organised around the health goals countries are pursuing, governed by
lines.6: clear principles, and built on shared, reusable components. It is not a prescriptive blueprint that
lines.7: mandates specific products or solutions. It is an adaptive framework — one that countries can
lines.8: engage with at the level that is relevant to them, using it to assess gaps, sequence investments,
lines.9: and make design decisions that are coherent with both their immediate context and their long-
lines.10: term aspirations. In doing so, it gives countries a coherent way to see how the parts of their
lines.11: digital health environment relate to one another and how individual investments contribute to the
lines.12: whole.
lines.13: Its contribution is to organise national infrastructure around shared, governed components —
lines.14: core registries and semantic and terminology services — connected through a standards-based
lines.15: means of exchange, so that the data health systems depend on become more consistent,
lines.16: trustworthy, and secure, and can be reused across programmes rather than rebuilt for each
lines.17: one. Better-governed data is the proximate benefit; it is what allows countries to plan, finance,
lines.18: and deliver health services with greater confidence.
lines.19: The reference architecture framework was developed using The Open Group ® Architecture
lines.20: Framework (TOGAF®) as its methodological foundation12. TOGAF® provides a structured,
lines.21: established approach to enterprise architecture that works from business goals through
lines.22: capabilities and application services that support them, to the technical components, so that
lines.23: architectural decisions remain traceable to the health goals they are intended to support. In
lines.24: practice this means a country can follow the chain in both directions: from any component or
lines.25: capability back to the health goal it serves, and forward to the specifications that govern its
lines.26: implementation. Where established frameworks and existing resources already cover part of
lines.27: this ground, they are referenced rather than duplicated.
lines.30: The reference architecture is set at the level of detail of a national health system. It describes
lines.31: the shared capabilities a national health system requires and the DPI-H components that deliver
lines.32: them. These components build on foundational DPI where it exists and are leveraged by the

lines.34: the architecture does not describe is the point-of-service applications and operational systems
lines.35: those programmes use to deliver their specific functions — electronic medical records, order-
lines.36: management platforms, warehouse-management tools, forecasting applications, and disease-
lines.37: specific programme tools. Such applications are important parts of a functioning digital health
lines.38: ecosystem, but they consume shared infrastructure rather than constitute it, and the architecture

lines.41: infrastructure that delivers one or more capabilities, not as a prescription to procure a specific
lines.43: Within this scope, the architecture organises DPI-H across two distinct but related layers.
lines.47: The first layer comprises the shared components that are reusable not only across health
lines.48: programmes but potentially across sectors. These establish authoritative, shared references for
lines.49: the people, places, products and services, and workers within the health system; maintain the
lines.50: longitudinal record of an individual's health and care; and provide the semantic and structural
lines.51: foundations that make data consistently meaningful across the ecosystem. The core registries
lines.52: — for clients (health service users), health facilities, health workers, and products — sit in this
lines.53: layer, alongside the lifelong health record, terminology services, and the logical information
lines.54: model repository. A practical test for whether a component belongs in this layer asks whether it
lines.55: can be reused across many health domains, exposes a clean and stable interface, avoids
lines.56: locking countries into domain-specific implementations, and supports a foundational capability
lines.57: rather than programme-specific logic. Components that meet these criteria belong here; those
lines.58: that do not, belong at the application layer, and the description of their functional requirements
lines.59: falls outside the scope of this reference architecture.
lines.62: The second layer describes a grouping of health capabilities that national health systems strive
lines.63: to deliver across their principal domains — clinical care, public health, the health supply chain,
lines.64: and health financing — together with the shared components that enable them. It sets out what
lines.65: countries need to achieve through the lens of the capabilities required for each business service
lines.66: first and then describes the shared components that the health system uses to realise those
lines.67: capabilities. Clinical care, for instance, draws on a computable decision support engine that
lines.68: evaluates a patient's health record against computable clinical guidelines to deliver
lines.69: recommendations, alerts, and risk assessments at the point of care; health financing draws on
lines.70: the Benefits Package Registry to support benefit design, eligibility, and claims; supply chain

lines.71: draws on a supplier registry to verify supplier credentials, inform procurement, and anchor
lines.72: product traceability; and public health and analytics services draw on health management
lines.73: information systems for programme monitoring and on public health surveillance platforms for
lines.74: outbreak detection and response. These business-service components build on the metadata
lines.75: registries and shared foundational components, and several serve more than one domain —
lines.76: health management information systems, for instance, support clinical quality monitoring,
lines.77: programme oversight, and financial accountability alike — which is what distinguishes shared
lines.79: Beyond the two layers, there are certain capabilities that are properties of DPI-H as a whole
lines.80: rather than features of any single component, layer, or business service. Interoperability is not
lines.81: a component to be built once but a property that should pervade the architecture through shared
lines.82: standards, common data models, and defined exchange patterns. Governance is cross-cutting
lines.83: in the same way: it applies to every component and capability the architecture describes and is
lines.84: treated as an architecture design principle below and elaborated on in the governance sub-
lines.87: The architecture does not redefine or duplicate what foundational DPI — digital identity,
lines.88: payments infrastructure, and general data exchange — provides. Where foundational DPI
lines.89: capabilities exist and are accessible, the architecture defines how DPI-H integrates with and
lines.90: builds upon them. Where they do not yet exist, it ensures that health systems can still function
lines.91: effectively in the present without being constrained by the absence of foundational DPI. This
lines.92: relationship is addressed in detail in the sub-chapters on DPI-H interoperability.
lines.93: Not all countries will implement the full scope of DPI-H at once, nor should they. Some
lines.94: capabilities and components form an essential foundation that every country should put in place

lines.99: 2.2 Resilient Essential Data and Digital Health
lines.101: 2.2.1 What REDDHI is and its foundational core
lines.102: Most countries embarking on digital health transformation do not start from a blank slate. They
lines.103: inherit vertical, often disease-specific programme systems, donor-funded tools, and legacy
lines.104: platforms, each designed to serve a specific function without reference to what else exists. Data
lines.105: is captured repeatedly across systems that cannot communicate, people and facilities are

lines.106: identified differently in each, and lists are rarely reconciled. The consequence is a fragmented
lines.107: ecosystem that burdens health workers, weakens the quality, trust, and security of the data
lines.108: available for use, and makes every new investment less productive than it should be.
lines.109: REDDHI — Resilient Essential Data and Digital Health Infrastructure — describes the direction
lines.110: of travel that addresses this fragmentation: a governed, interoperable digital health
lines.111: infrastructure built on open standards and trusted, secure, quality data, within which local and
lines.112: regional innovation can flourish, investments can be mobilised and absorbed at scale, and the
lines.113: health system can sustain itself technically and financially over time. It is not a fixed destination
lines.114: to be reached and signed off, and it is not a set of systems to procure. It is a condition of self-
lines.115: sustaining national digital health maturity that continues to evolve as needs and technology
lines.116: change — one in which the foundational capabilities every health programme depends upon are
lines.117: shared, interoperable, and governed in the public interest rather than duplicated in silos.
lines.118: A country does not need the whole of REDDHI in place to begin. The starting point can be a
lines.119: core set of metadata registries, the (lifelong) health record, and the means to exchange data
lines.120: between them; These registries are interdependent: a longitudinal record carries little weight
lines.121: without the means to establish where and by whom each entry was made, so the facility and
lines.122: health workforce registries are what allow the provenance of records to be established, just as
lines.123: the client registry is what allows them to be reliably attributed to the right individual. REDDHI is
lines.124: the broader, maturing state those foundations make possible. Countries do not become
lines.125: “REDDHI-compliant” at a point in time; rather, they can gauge progress through observable
lines.126: markers — whether authoritative registries exist and are reused across programmes, whether
lines.127: data is exchanged through governed, standards-based means, and whether the quality and
lines.128: stewardship of that data are actively managed. Framed this way, REDDHI gives countries a way
lines.129: to assess their current state, identify gaps, and ground architectural choices in health-system
lines.130: requirements rather than in whatever technology happens to be available.
lines.131: This interdependence is what defines the essential core: the capabilities whose absence
lines.132: imposes the greatest cost on the rest of the ecosystem, and which, once in place, make every
lines.133: other investment more connectable and more sustainable. The table below summarises these
lines.134: foundational capabilities and the DPI-H components that deliver them. Most of these capabilities
lines.135: form the minimum viable foundation that countries should prioritise regardless of starting point;
lines.136: other capabilities such as having consistent data structures across systems are typically built up
lines.137: from that foundation as maturity grows. The full mapping of capabilities to components across
lines.138: all seven priority health goals is set out in the methodology section that follows and the defining
lines.139: characteristics of DPI-H application components are described in the DPI-H application

lines.181: The DPI-H reference architecture is guided by a set of principles intended to ensure that
lines.182: national digital health architectures are sustainable, interoperable, and responsive to country
lines.183: needs. The architecture is context-adaptive, recognising variations in digital readiness,
lines.184: institutional capacity, and resource availability, and it acknowledges differing policy, legislative,
lines.185: and governance models without favouring a single approach.
lines.187: Whereas the DPI-H principles established earlier define the character of health digital public
lines.188: infrastructure, the architecture design principles below translate those commitments into the
lines.189: design decisions and structural choices that shape how the architecture should be built and
lines.190: implemented in practice. The two are intended to be read together: each architectural design
lines.191: principle translates a DPI-H principle into the design decisions and constraints that put it into
lines.192: practice, and together providing the criteria against which design decisions should be tested.
lines.195: Countries should ensure that architectural decisions reflect and reinforce clear
lines.196: governance frameworks at every level — from the stewardship of individual DPI-H
lines.197: components to the oversight of the broader health digital ecosystem— with defined
lines.198: accountability structures, clear ownership of shared infrastructure, and arrangements
lines.199: proportionate to the sensitivity and criticality of the capabilities they oversee.
lines.200: Governance is a foundational architectural activity that precedes and shapes technical
lines.201: decisions rather than a project-level concern addressed after implementation, and it
lines.202: should not be assumed to be inherited from the frameworks or reference architectures a
lines.205: A critical dimension of governance is the stewardship of data quality within shared
lines.206: components. Data quality is not only a top-down control mechanism but also a matter of
lines.207: relevance, accuracy, and fitness for purpose, sustained by the stakeholders who
lines.208: contribute to and rely on the data. The value of shared health infrastructure depends on
lines.209: the accuracy, completeness, timeliness, and consistency of the data it holds, and
lines.210: weaknesses cascade across clinical data exchange, public health surveillance, supply
lines.211: chain management, health financing, and workforce planning. Those who bear the data-
lines.212: entry burden often do not see the benefit of the resulting quality, so countries should
lines.213: design feedback such that contributors gain value from the data they enter, and should
lines.214: set minimum data-quality requirements as a governance prerequisite before a shared
lines.217: As a design principle, this means governance arrangements shape architectural choices
lines.218: rather than follow them: components are designed with clear ownership and
lines.219: accountability built in, with access and decision rights that can be enforced technically
lines.220: and set proportionate to the sensitivity of the data, and with the stewardship of data

lines.221: quality described above designed into each shared component from the outset. The
lines.222: institutional and semantic governance arrangements through which countries exercise
lines.223: this oversight are set out in the governance chapter (Section 3.4).
lines.227: Countries should ground their DPI-H implementations in open standards and
lines.228: specifications developed through recognised Standards Development Organisations and
lines.229: open governance processes. Open standards promote interoperability, portability, and
lines.230: transparency, and reduce dependency on proprietary technology. In applying this
lines.231: principle, countries should distinguish between recommending open standards and
lines.232: requiring every setting to implement them in the same way and to the same degree
lines.233: regardless of local readiness. The architecture points to FHIR-based approaches as the
lines.234: direction of travel, while accommodating countries at different stages of readiness:
lines.235: distribution of terminology, information models, and registry data can use APIs,
lines.236: subscription mechanisms, or lighter-weight formats in lower-readiness contexts,
lines.237: provided a clear progression path toward open-standards compliance is established and
lines.241: Countries should treat interoperability as a structural property of their architecture, not an
lines.242: integration challenge to be solved after systems are built. The ability to exchange and
lines.243: use data meaningfully — across health sector systems and with foundational DPI —
lines.244: should be designed in from the outset through shared standards, common data models,
lines.245: and defined integration patterns. Interoperability should not be architected solely around
lines.246: a single centralised mediator: centralised middleware can create bottlenecks, single
lines.247: points of failure, and concentrations of control that undermine resilience and
lines.248: governance. Countries should be open to decentralised models in which each system
lines.249: carries its own interoperability capability, with the interoperability layer defined as a
lines.250: distributed architectural capability rather than a monolithic central component. Federated
lines.251: implementations, in which data remains where it is generated and is accessed or
lines.252: aggregated on demand, are a natural expression of this approach and are supported by
lines.253: the reference architecture — and they are particularly useful in environments where
lines.254: continuous central connectivity cannot be assumed, allowing systems to operate and
lines.255: exchange data without depending on a permanent connection to a central point.
lines.257: Architectural decisions that defer interoperability to a later phase, or that create
lines.258: centralised dependencies as the only integration mechanism, can generate technical
lines.259: and political debt that becomes increasingly costly to resolve as the ecosystem grows.
lines.260: Designing for interoperability therefore means treating its requirements as something
lines.261: that evolves rather than is fixed once; as needs on the ground change, the architecture
lines.262: should accommodate proactive change management rather than locking countries into
lines.263: the integration decisions of the moment.

lines.267: Countries should make architectural choices that can be sustained over the long term,
lines.268: both financially and technically. As a design principle, this means evaluating options
lines.269: against their whole-of-life cost and viability — to build, operate, maintain, and evolve —
lines.270: rather than the cost to stand them up; an approach that is inexpensive to deploy but
lines.271: cannot be maintained, or that goes unused, is not a sustainable choice however low its
lines.272: initial cost. Design decisions should be weighed against whether they continue to deliver
lines.273: value across the changes of government, funding, and priorities that any national system
lines.276: Financially, this means designing a national architecture for shared investment rather
lines.277: than duplicated effort — favouring components that can be reused across programmes
lines.278: over ones procured separately for each — and designing shared infrastructure so that its
lines.279: short-, medium-, and long-term value can be demonstrated to those whose continued
lines.280: commitment sustains it. Technically, it means favouring standards, technologies, and
lines.281: implementation approaches that in-country teams can maintain, extend, and evolve
lines.282: without prohibitive cost or reliance on scarce external expertise — a consideration that
lines.283: weighs more heavily where national digital infrastructure is still developing.
lines.287: Countries should adopt a modular approach, building capabilities incrementally from
lines.288: their current state rather than treating full implementation as a prerequisite for value. As
lines.289: a design principle, this means giving each component clear boundaries and a well-
lines.290: defined interface, so that components are loosely coupled — able to be developed,
lines.291: deployed, replaced, or upgraded independently, without requiring changes to the others
lines.292: that rely on them. A component whose internal workings are entangled with those
lines.293: around it cannot be adopted, adapted, or evolved on its own, which is what modularity is
lines.296: Designed this way, the reference architecture is aspirational in direction but pragmatic in
lines.297: entry point – countries can see themselves in it regardless of where they start, and can
lines.298: adopt the components relevant to them without implementing the whole architecture first.
lines.299: The minimum viable foundation for DPI-H provides a clear, bounded starting point from
lines.300: which capabilities are extended over time, and individual components can be piloted,
lines.301: evaluated, and iterated without disrupting the wider architecture.
lines.305: Countries should treat the development and retention of in-country technical capacity as
lines.306: an explicit architectural consideration, not a training matter addressed after the
lines.307: architecture is built. As a design principle, this means selecting standards, technologies,
lines.308: and implementation approaches that local teams can realistically understand, operate,

lines.309: and extend — favouring widely supported, well-documented technologies over
lines.310: specialised or closed technologies whose inner workings are not visible to the teams
lines.311: expected to run them — and designing the architecture to be transparent in how it is
lines.312: structured and governed, through documentation and openly published specifications, so
lines.313: that the people who run it can reason about it and build on it. Design choices that
lines.314: expose how components work, rather than hiding them behind proprietary boundaries,
lines.315: are what allow capability to take root and remain in-country.
lines.317: An architecture that a country cannot understand, operate, and evolve with its own
lines.318: people is not genuinely owned by it, whatever the formal arrangements say, and reliance
lines.319: on external expertise that cannot be substituted locally is a standing risk to continuity.
lines.320: Technology selection, documentation, and the design of operational tooling should
lines.321: therefore be weighed for local operability, so that capability is built and retained rather
lines.326: Countries should design their DPI-H architecture to serve all populations equitably,
lines.327: including those in remote, under-resourced, or marginalised settings. At the level of the
lines.328: architecture, this is a structural concern and it shapes how the architecture as a whole is
lines.329: arranged so that the populations and settings least well served are not designed out of it.
lines.331: The following design decisions give this effect:
lines.332: • The architecture should scale to context — designed so that the capability
lines.333: required to participate matches the resources of different settings, allowing it to
lines.334: be implemented and operated where infrastructure, connectivity, and institutional
lines.335: capacity are limited, not only where they are abundant.
lines.336: • It should degrade gracefully rather than exclude. The absence of a given
lines.337: foundational layer — continuous connectivity, a mature national identity system,
lines.338: particular infrastructure — should reduce what is available rather than lock a
lines.339: setting or a population out entirely, so that participation does not depend on
lines.340: prerequisites that the least-served cannot meet.
lines.342: The architecture's responsibility is to be structured so that serving the least-served is
lines.343: possible and coherent across the system rather than exceptional.
lines.346: VIII. Data Ownership, Access, and Control
lines.347: Countries should ensure that their architectural choices give concrete expression to the
lines.348: rights of individuals over their personal health data, and to the rights of public entities
lines.349: over the infrastructure and data they depend on. Consent management, access controls,
lines.350: and data governance should be enforceable, transparent, and meaningful in practice.
lines.351: Architectural decisions around storage, exchange, and access should default to data

lines.352: minimisation, purpose limitation, and individual agency, with any departure justified
lines.355: Consent is the primary mechanism through which individuals exercise these rights — the
lines.356: ability to give, withhold, and withdraw permission for health information to be accessed
lines.357: and shared. As health information becomes increasingly digital and longitudinal — held
lines.358: in personal health records and exchanged across facilities and programmes — a shared
lines.359: means of recording and acting on an individual's consent preferences grows more
lines.360: important. Without it, the broader aims of individual access to health information and
lines.361: meaningful control over its use are difficult to realise in practice.
lines.363: As a design principle, this means designing the architecture so that consent, where it is
lines.364: captured, can be represented in a common, standards-based form and carried with the
lines.365: data it governs as that data moves between systems. Whether and how that consent is
lines.366: then enforced rests with the systems that hold and exchange the data and with the legal
lines.367: and governance framework that applies to them. The architecture does not set the rules
lines.368: that govern consent — what constitutes a valid consent, who is entitled to grant or
lines.369: withdraw it, or what rights of access apply — which are matters for each country's law
lines.370: and policy and vary considerably between settings. Where a country has consent
lines.371: infrastructure that operates across sectors, the health sector should consider building on
lines.372: it rather than creating a parallel capability, in keeping with the architecture's approach of
lines.373: leveraging foundational digital public infrastructure where it exists. Cross-sector consent
lines.374: infrastructure remains uncommon, however, and the sensitivity of health data and the
lines.375: governance arrangements around it often give rise to health-specific requirements.
lines.376: Where this is so, a health-sector consent capability may be needed, designed to
lines.377: interoperate with national infrastructure should it later become available. Established
lines.378: references such as the IHE privacy and consent profiles and the HL7 FHIR Consent
lines.379: resource offer a starting point for how consent can be represented and exchanged.
lines.381: Public health infrastructure is increasingly built and operated through a mix of public,
lines.382: private, donor, and partner arrangements, and a government can hold formal ownership
lines.383: of a system while lacking the practical ability to access its data, modify it, or move away
lines.384: from the supplier that runs it. The architecture should be designed so that this practical
lines.385: control sits with the public entity by default — through open standards, documented
lines.386: interfaces, data portability, and clear separation between the data a country owns and
lines.387: the systems that process it — so that a country can exercise genuine control over its
lines.388: essential infrastructure and data, rather than that control being constrained by the
lines.389: arrangements through which those systems are funded and operated.
lines.393: A health system that shares data across many systems and institutions can only do so
lines.394: on the basis of trust: participants exchange information when they can be confident that
lines.395: the systems they exchange it with are what they claim to be, that the data is genuine and

lines.396: unaltered, and that sensitive information will be protected. Trust is a property the
lines.397: architecture has to be designed to establish and sustain across every component and
lines.398: exchange, and it underpins the trusted, secure data on which every other capability
lines.401: As a design principle, this means designing the architecture so that data is accessed
lines.402: and exchanged only between participants whose identity and authorisation can be
lines.403: verified. Authorisation in this sense being the right to access or act under the applicable
lines.404: rules is distinct from an individual's consent, which is addressed under the data
lines.405: ownership principle. It means designing so that the origin and authenticity of data and
lines.406: documents can be established; and so that confidentiality is preserved in transit and at
lines.407: rest. And it means designing the architecture so that the compromise of any single
lines.408: component is contained rather than able to cascade across the wider system.
lines.410: Security cannot be expressed as a single fixed standard, because countries differ widely
lines.411: in their security regulations, skills, and infrastructure. Countries should design for
lines.412: graduated levels of assurance, adopting security measures matched to their context —
lines.413: beginning, where necessary, with simpler or manual checks and strengthening toward
lines.414: digital signatures and cryptographic provenance as capability grows — rather than
lines.415: treating a single level of security as a precondition for progress. Where a country has
lines.416: national trust infrastructure, such as public key infrastructure, certificate authorities, and
lines.417: digital signature or verifiable-credential services, the health sector can build on it rather
lines.418: than establish a parallel basis for trust. Where such infrastructure is not yet in place, the
lines.419: architecture should allow countries to proceed with the assurance available to them,
lines.420: while being clear about the risks that operating without a foundational basis for trust
lines.421: entails. In all cases, the strength of security measures should be proportionate to the
lines.422: sensitivity and criticality of the data and the capability they protect.
lines.424: Trust and security are also conditions of resilience: infrastructure that cannot protect
lines.425: itself, or that fails entirely when one part is compromised, cannot be relied upon. The
lines.426: specific controls, configurations, and operational practices through which these design
lines.427: decisions are realised rest with implementation and with each country's security policy.
lines.430: Countries should treat the ethical implications of their architectural choices as design
lines.431: considerations in their own right, not as matters to be settled separately from how the
lines.432: infrastructure is built. Health data is among the most sensitive information a person
lines.433: generates, and the way the architecture is designed shapes what can be done with that
lines.434: data, by whom, and to whose benefit or harm.
lines.436: As a design principle, this means designing the architecture to prevent misuse of health
lines.437: and health-related data, with use confined to defined and legitimate purposes and
lines.438: sensitive information protected from exposure. Where data is put to secondary use — for
lines.439: analytics, research, or training AI models — the architecture should be designed so that

lines.440: this rests on appropriately de-identified or privacy-protected data, remains bound to
lines.441: defined and transparent purposes, and does not expose individuals or communities to
lines.442: harm or disadvantage, including at the level of groups and populations rather than
lines.443: individuals alone. Transparency about what data is collected, how it is used, and who

lines.452: 2.4 Methodology: Mapping Health Goals to DPI-H
lines.453: The seven priority health goals that underpin this reference architecture were systematically
lines.454: mapped to the digital capabilities and foundational components required to achieve them. This
lines.455: mapping is the methodological backbone of the architecture, and it provides the consolidated
lines.456: account of how goals translate into component choices.
lines.457: The architecture was designed from the perspective of what the health system needs to
lines.458: achieve, rather than from the perspective of what technologies exist. This matters because a
lines.459: goals-first approach differs from technology-led design. Technology-led design begins with the
lines.460: technologies or components available and works outward to what they enable; a goals-first
lines.461: approach begins from the health outcomes a country is accountable for and works toward the
lines.462: shared infrastructure those goals require. While capability-based, goals-driven approaches are
lines.463: established in enterprise architecture, their rigorous application to national-scale digital health

lines.464: infrastructure — deriving components from health-system goals rather than from a catalogue of
lines.465: technologies — is a meaningful departure from how such architectures have often been
lines.467: The mapping was conducted using a TOGAF-based approach, working top-down from health
lines.468: goals through stakeholder value, business capabilities, application services, and application
lines.469: components, while simultaneously working bottom-up from known DPI-H components and
lines.470: existing digital health infrastructure. The convergence of these two directions produced a
lines.471: requirements picture grounded in both what countries need to achieve and what is
lines.472: implementable through shared infrastructure, keeping the architecture simultaneously
lines.474: A consistent finding across all seven goals is that the same foundational components recur. The
lines.475: client registry, for example, is required across trusted personal health records, quality and
lines.476: continuity of care, public health and disease surveillance, and health financing; the facility
lines.477: registry is equally cross-cutting. This convergence is what distinguishes DPI-H components
lines.478: from programme-specific tools, and it confirms not just which components belong in shared
lines.479: infrastructure but why they warrant investment as such.
lines.480: Equally consistent is that these shared components do not, on their own, deliver the outcome.
lines.481: The outcome is delivered when point-of-service and functional applications — the systems
lines.482: clinicians, programme managers, and administrators actually use — draw on that shared
lines.483: infrastructure to do the work. The architecture defines and governs the shared components; it
lines.484: enables the applications that consume them rather than defining those applications. Each goal
lines.485: therefore depends on both: shared infrastructure for consistency and reuse, and the
lines.486: applications that turn it into delivered services.

lines.491: • what the health system should be able to do to achieve it, described in technology-
lines.493: • the capabilities this requires, mapped to the DPI-H components that deliver them and
lines.495: • how those components are reused across other goals, reinforcing the case for shared

lines.498: Equitable Health Financing — is set out below as a worked example. The same structure has

lines.2: The reference architecture translates the analytical work of the health goals mapping into a
lines.3: structured description that countries can use to design, assess, and sequence their digital health
lines.4: infrastructure investments. It is intended to help national teams and implementers plan, build, and
lines.5: evaluate health information systems that are interoperable, scalable, and aligned with established
lines.6: practice. By offering a common vocabulary and a shared structural model, it supports consistent
lines.7: description, comparison, and assessment of digital health architectures across different contexts
lines.8: and implementations. Its purpose is to connect health goals to the capabilities that serve them
lines.9: and the shared infrastructure that realises them, keeping investment decisions anchored to health
lines.10: outcomes rather than to the solutions that happen to be available.
lines.11: It is a reference model to be adapted, not a prescriptive architecture that countries must adhere
lines.12: to. It offers a common vocabulary and a set of elements from which each country composes an
lines.13: architecture suited to its own context — adopting, extending, or setting aside elements as local
lines.14: priorities and constraints require.
lines.15: This chapter is organised as follows:
lines.16: • Section 3.1 describes the modelling approach and the shared language used to express
lines.17: the architecture.
lines.18: • Section 3.2 explains how to read and navigate the reference architecture, which is
lines.19: maintained as a living model rather than a fixed picture.
lines.20: • Section 3.3 illustrates the approach through worked examples for some health goals.
lines.21: • Section 3.4 sets out the governance arrangements that surround the architecture.
lines.22: • Section 3.5 introduces the DPI-H application components, whose full descriptions are
lines.23: provided in appendix C.
lines.24: • Section 3.6 describes the interoperability architecture within DPI-H, through which these
lines.25: components work together as a coherent ecosystem
lines.27: An architecture describes a system in terms of its elements, the relationships among them, and
lines.28: the principles guiding its design and evolution. For architectures to be compared or assessed
lines.29: against one another, they need a shared way of describing these things: agreed types of
lines.30: elements, agreed types of relationship between them, and consistent rules for how they fit
lines.31: together. Where such a shared description is absent, familiar terms such as “component”,
lines.32: “service”, and “capability” can carry different meanings in different settings, which makes
lines.33: systematic comparison difficult and limits the value of cross-country analysis.

lines.34: Rather than define a new vocabulary, the reference architecture is expressed using ArchiMate ®,
lines.35: an open modelling language for enterprise architecture maintained by The Open Group. 2
lines.36: ArchiMate® provides defined types of element — among them goals, capabilities, services,
lines.37: application components, and data objects — and defined types of relationship between them,
lines.38: organised across business, application, and technology layers — broadly aligning with the
lines.39: architecture domains of established enterprise-architecture practice1 — together with motivation
lines.40: elements that capture why an element matters and to whom. Drawing on an established language
lines.41: brings several practical benefits. Each element has a defined type with clear meaning, so that a
lines.42: capability, a component, and a service are not confused with one another. The architecture can
lines.43: be authored, checked, and published using widely available tools. Because the language is
lines.44: broadly adopted, descriptions expressed in it can be read and compared across organisations
lines.45: and countries without translation. And the typed relationships make it possible to trace from goals,
lines.46: through the capabilities that serve them, to the components that realise them — a property that
lines.47: matters for governance and for assessing whether the architecture is delivering on its goals.
lines.48: On that note, it is worth drawing out the following points, because they shape how the rest of the
lines.50: • First, the architecture is more than a set of concepts: it is the way those concepts are
lines.51: articulated. An element is defined in part by what it depends on and what depends on it,
lines.52: and much of the value of the description comes from these relationships being made
lines.53: explicit and kept consistent. Expressing the architecture in a formal language in this way
lines.54: turns it into a set of criteria against which a candidate architecture can, in time, be checked
lines.55: for completeness and consistency, and from which a country-specific architecture can be
lines.56: derived rather than assembled from scratch.
lines.57: • Second, only a subset of the available element and relationship types is used here —
lines.58: those relevant to the scope of DPI-H. The remainder of the modelling language is not
lines.59: required for this purpose and is not used.

lines.223: Governance is the set of arrangements through which decision authority is distributed,
lines.224: exercised and accounted for across all those who depend upon, contribute to, or are served by
lines.225: the shared infrastructure. It is not principally an administrative function but rather the means by
lines.226: which shared infrastructure remains trustworthy, financially sustainable and equitable over time,
lines.227: and through which the architecture continues to deliver the semantic consistency and reliability
lines.228: the rest of this guidance depends upon.
lines.230: Because DPI-H is shared infrastructure — relied upon and contributed to by many actors, and
lines.231: serving the health system as a whole rather than any single programme or institution —
lines.232: governance attends both to the strategic direction of the shared infrastructure and to its day-to-
lines.233: day operational integrity. These are distinct responsibilities calling for distinct structures, though
lines.234: they operate in close coordination. A consistent theme across the development of this architecture
lines.235: is that this coordination, and the institutional arrangements behind it, come before technology
lines.236: rather than after it: countries that establish authoritative registries, harmonise their core data, and
lines.237: agree who decides what tend to progress, while those that begin from application components
lines.238: without these arrangements tend to fragment.

lines.239: This section describes governance principles and structural characteristics applicable to national
lines.240: and regional DPI-H deployments. The specific structures — the composition of bodies, decision
lines.241: procedures and accountability mechanisms — are determined by each country or regional
lines.242: implementation in accordance with its legal, institutional and political context. Where examples
lines.243: are provided, they are illustrative rather than prescriptive. The same separation holds for the
lines.244: shared data assets the architecture defines: the registries are described elsewhere in this
lines.245: guidance as authoritative, canonical constructs governed by a single accountable source, while
lines.246: the question of whether they are realised centrally, in a federated manner, or as a hybrid remains
lines.247: a national implementation choice. Governance, in this sense, is a policy matter; implementation
lines.250: The following principles should guide the governance design of any national DPI-H deployment:
lines.251: • Subsidiarity. Decision authority should sit at the lowest level at which it can be exercised
lines.252: effectively. Operational decisions should not require strategic deliberation, and strategic
lines.253: decisions should not be delegated to operational bodies.
lines.254: • Separation of mandate and execution. Strategic governance sets direction, defines scope
lines.255: boundaries and safeguards the long-term viability of the infrastructure; operational
lines.256: governance executes within those boundaries and has defined pathways to escalate when
lines.258: • Inclusive representation. Governance structures should actively represent the
lines.259: communities most dependent on the infrastructure and least able to advocate for themselves
lines.260: through conventional political or market processes — including rural populations, women,
lines.261: displaced persons, and those served by under-resourced health systems. Representation of
lines.262: this kind should be more than advisory; governance design should give the interests of these
lines.263: communities genuine weight in strategic decisions, not nominal inclusion only. Translating
lines.264: nominal representation into real influence is a persistent challenge, and the mechanisms for
lines.265: pursuing it are set out in 3.4.3.
lines.266: • Financial sustainability as a governance mandate. Digital health experience shows that
lines.267: technically promising systems often fail to sustain or scale when they remain dependent on
lines.268: short-term project funding, underestimated operating costs, weak institutional ownership, or
lines.269: insufficient integration into routine health system operations.18,19,20 Governance should
lines.270: therefore treat the financial continuity of shared infrastructure not as a downstream
lines.271: implementation concern but as a core strategic mandate, with defined accountability,
lines.273: • Prevention of resource overuse. Shared digital infrastructure should be governed so that
lines.274: no single programme, institution, vendor, or user group can place disproportionate demand
lines.275: on shared capacity, support resources, or operating budgets in ways that reduce service
lines.276: quality for others. Governance should establish usage policies, contribution expectations,

lines.292: what the infrastructure exists to achieve, who it serves, what is within and outside its scope, and
lines.293: how resources are secured and allocated to sustain it. It does not manage operations; it creates
lines.294: the mandate within which operations function. Its responsibilities include:
lines.295: • establishing and maintaining the infrastructure's mission, scope and core values;
lines.296: • safeguarding financial and institutional sustainability across funding cycles;
lines.297: • approving major architectural or strategic changes that cross organisational boundaries
lines.299: • ensuring that underserved and underrepresented communities have genuine voice in its
lines.301: • monitoring for systemic risks such as resource overuse, inequitable access and
lines.303: • defining the escalation triggers and response protocols for issues that exceed the
lines.307: Three of the principles in 3.4.2 are substantive rather than procedural: they concern what the
lines.308: shared infrastructure should remain — adequately funded, equitable in whom it serves, and
lines.309: protected from overuse. These are the ways shared public infrastructure most characteristically
lines.310: fails, and stating them as principles does not secure them; a principle does not fund the
lines.311: infrastructure, give underserved groups a place in governance, or cap anyone's usage.
