lines.374: The metadata registries that form the foundation of DPI-H — the client, health facility, health
lines.375: workforce and product registries, the Terminology Service, and the Logical Information Model
lines.376: Repository — are only as reliable as the governance that maintains them. A Terminology Service
lines.377: can be deployed and operational, and a Logical Information Model Repository can hold a rich
lines.378: catalogue of national data structures, yet without sustained, structured governance over how
lines.379: these assets are created, versioned, reviewed, published and distributed, the infrastructure they
lines.380: provide becomes progressively unreliable. In real implementations, countries have encountered
lines.381: concepts deprecated without notice, version conflicts between systems, and national
lines.382: implementation guides drifting from the models they were derived from. The reference
lines.383: architecture introduces the Semantic Governance Infrastructure (SGI) to address these
lines.384: failures: it is the cross-cutting capability that keeps the metadata registry components accurate,
lines.385: consistent and trustworthy, so that the semantic consistency they are intended to provide does
lines.386: not degrade as the health digital ecosystem grows.
lines.387: A governance capability, not a technical component
lines.388: Before describing how it works, it is important to be clear about what SGI is and is not. It is not a
lines.389: new software product or a centralised technical component, and it is not an information-
lines.390: technology concern to be delegated to a systems team. It is a cross-cutting capability —
lines.391: predominantly a matter of institutions, roles and processes — through which a health system
lines.392: governs the meaning of its data. The stakeholders who submit change requests, review and
lines.393: approve content, maintain national extensions of global standards, and ensure that local clinical
lines.394: reality is reflected in nationally governed models are as essential to SGI as any software.
lines.395: Experience in comparable settings shows that governance often runs on tools that were not

lines.396: purpose-built for it, and that the quality of the process depends far more on the clarity of roles,
lines.397: decision rights and workflows than on the sophistication of the technology. Countries should
lines.398: therefore invest first in the committees, roles, decision rights and community processes of
lines.399: governance, and only afterwards in tooling.
lines.400: SGI is distinct from runtime services
lines.401: This governance capability is distinct from the runtime services that operate alongside it. A
lines.402: Terminology Service deployed to support clinical data capture performs a runtime function —
lines.403: vocabulary lookups, validation of coded entries, and distribution of value sets to consuming
lines.404: systems. SGI operates at a different level: it determines what content those services hold, how it
lines.405: is reviewed and approved, when it is published, how change is managed, and how consuming
lines.406: systems are notified. The two are complementary and mutually necessary: runtime services
lines.407: without governance produce content that cannot be trusted, while governance without runtime
lines.408: services produces decisions that cannot be operationalised. This integrated, cross-registry
lines.409: governance layer is a new aspect that DPI-H introduces. Existing health information architecture
lines.410: specifications, including OpenHIE, specify the runtime terminology service but not the cross-
lines.411: registry semantic-governance described here — the coordinated review workflows, multi-
lines.412: stakeholder curation, release management and harmonisation flows between global, national and
lines.413: local content that span the Terminology Service, the Logical Information Model Repository and
lines.414: national data models together. SGI is therefore presented as cross-cutting rather than a
lines.415: component of any single registry, because its scope spans all of the metadata registry
lines.416: components and because its processes need to be coherent across them rather than managed

lines.453: Countries need not achieve full semantic governance maturity before deploying metadata
lines.454: registries, and the appropriate starting point varies considerably by context. In highly regulated
lines.455: settings — where data structures may be encoded in legislation — a comprehensive governance
lines.456: framework may need to be established before deployment proceeds. In many lower-resource
lines.457: settings, deployment can and should precede full governance maturity, with governance
lines.458: capabilities built incrementally as the ecosystem develops. A maturity-spectrum approach is
lines.459: therefore appropriate, progressing from minimal reference-list management, through structured
lines.460: versioning and change workflows, to fully governed, multi-stakeholder terminology and
lines.461: information-model ecosystems. What matters from the outset is that early deployment decisions
lines.462: do not close off the path to stronger governance later, and that a clear direction of travel is
lines.463: established even where immediate capacity is limited. Established terminology-governance
lines.464: maturity models can be applied, with some abstraction, across the metadata registry components.

lines.544: 3.5.1 What Distinguishes a DPI-H Application Component
lines.545: Not every digital system in a national health ecosystem qualifies as DPI-H. An application
lines.546: component earns that designation by meeting a specific set of criteria that distinguish shared
lines.547: public infrastructure from programme-specific tools or functional applications. The design of a
lines.548: DPI-H component satisfies the core DPI-H principles, and the following defining characteristics
lines.549: further distinguish them from other digital health applications and services:

lines.550: • Reusability across multiple health programmes and use cases without modification to
lines.552: • Ability to expose stable, standards-based interfaces that allow any conformant system
lines.553: to connect to it without requiring bespoke integration.
lines.554: • Ability to support foundational health system functions rather than programme-
lines.555: specific logic and serve the ecosystem as a whole rather than a single programme's
lines.557: • They should be publicly governed, ensuring that no single programme, donor, or
lines.558: vendor controls access to or evolution of the capability it provides.
lines.559: • They should be governed across their lifecycle — backed by clear governance
lines.560: arrangements for its deployment, operation, and evolution, distinct from the question of
lines.562: • They should be non-transactional — not point-of-care workflow engines or clinical
lines.563: transaction processors, but enabling infrastructure that orchestrates national-level data
lines.564: and makes it available to the systems that do perform those functions.
lines.565: • They should be functionally stable. In essence, their core function and interface
lines.566: specifications should be designed to remain consistent over time, providing a reliable
lines.567: foundation that operational applications and clinical systems can depend upon without
lines.568: being disrupted by changes in those systems.
lines.569: • They should be technology-neutral. Meaning that they should be specified at the level
lines.570: of function and capability rather than implementation, so that countries can choose the
lines.571: technology through which a component is delivered without being constrained to a
lines.574: These characteristics have practical consequences for what countries invest in and govern
lines.575: collectively. An application component that meets them justifies shared investment and shared
lines.576: governance. One that does not — however useful — belongs at the functional application layer,
lines.577: drawing on shared infrastructure rather than constituting it.

unnumbered: Box 3.1: Criteria for DPI-H Application Components
DPI-H should serve as a shared layer upon which multiple functional applications, point-of-
service and programme-specific systems depend. DPI-H application components should:
• Be reusable across multiple health programmes and use cases without modification to
its core design
• Expose stable, standards-based interfaces that allow any conformant system to
connect without bespoke integration
• Support foundational health system functions rather than programme-specific logic
• Be publicly governed — no single programme, donor, or vendor controls access or
evolution
• Be governed across its lifecycle — have clear governance frameworks that guide
deployment, operation, and evolution
• Be non-transactional — not a point-of-care workflow engine, but enabling
infrastructure that orchestrates national-level data

lines.723: The delivery of healthcare involves many actors — ministries and their programmes, public and
lines.724: private facilities, clinicians and community health workers, laboratories and pharmacies, supply
lines.725: chain operators, health coverage schemes, researchers, and the people receiving care — each
lines.726: holding part of the information another needs, and each with its own informational requirements.
lines.727: No single system can hold all of this, and none should attempt to. Interoperability is the property
lines.728: that allows these distinct systems to share information through common standards and agreed

lines.729: exchange mechanisms, so that data, wherever it is accessed across the health ecosystem, is
lines.730: timely, secure, clinically meaningful and usable for the purpose at hand.26
lines.732: Interoperability, therefore, is a cross-cutting capability of the reference architecture as a whole,
lines.733: rather than a single component a country procures or a discrete layer it installs. It is realised
lines.734: through several complementary things working together: shared content and terminology
lines.735: standards; governed information models; agreed exchange patterns; and the foundational trust
lines.736: and transport services on which exchange depends. It is helpful to distinguish the recognised
lines.737: dimensions along which interoperability is achieved in healthcare — the technical ability to move
lines.738: data between systems; the structural consistency of how that data is organised; the semantic
lines.739: preservation of what the data means; and the organisational and governance arrangements,
lines.740: including legal basis, consent and data-sharing agreements, that make exchange lawful and
lines.741: trusted.27 Technical exchange without structural, semantic and organisational interoperability
lines.742: moves data that the receiving system is unable to interpret or act upon safely. This section
lines.743: therefore addresses all of these dimensions rather than transport alone.
lines.745: 3.6.1 Interoperability as a capability, not just a component
lines.747: Earlier health information exchange architectures, including the widely adopted OpenHIE
lines.748: specification, describe an interoperability layer that acts as the single point of entry to the
lines.749: exchange — orchestrating transactions, routing messages, authenticating the application
lines.750: components that connect, and maintaining a central audit trail.28 These remain valuable
lines.751: functions. Experience across countries has shown, however, that depicting interoperability as
lines.752: one box in an architectural diagram is frequently read by ministries and implementing teams as
lines.753: a single piece of software that has to be bought, hosted and operated centrally; and that this
lines.754: tends to produce exactly the concentration of control, single points of failure and procurement
lines.755: bottlenecks that a digital public-infrastructure approach seeks to avoid. This guidance
lines.756: accordingly presents interoperability as a capability that pervades the architecture, expressed
lines.757: as a single capability in the architecture, and realised in implementation through whatever
lines.758: combination of mechanisms a country's context requires.
lines.760: A related distinction matters for clarity. Connecting two digital applications directly through an
lines.761: agreed message format achieves integration, but not necessarily interoperability.
lines.762: Interoperability, in its true sense, rests on open, publicly governed specifications that any
lines.763: conforming application component can implement, enabling one-to-many reuse and economies
lines.764: of scale rather than a proliferation of bilateral connections that accumulate technical debt and do
lines.765: not scale nationally. The objective of the architecture is interoperability in this stronger sense:
lines.766: shared specifications, openly governed, to which systems conform at their boundaries.

lines.802: The architecture locates these two concerns in two foundational DPI-H components described
lines.803: elsewhere in this guidance. The Terminology Service governs meaning: the codes, value sets
lines.804: and classifications — drawn from, and mapped across, international vocabularies — by which
lines.805: clinical and administrative concepts are represented and interpreted consistently. The Logical
lines.806: Information Model Repository governs structure: the logical information models that define how
lines.807: data is organised and contextualised, maintained as governed, versioned national assets. The
lines.808: two are often summarised by analogy as the dictionary and the grammar of health data; both
lines.809: are required for data to be exchanged with its meaning preserved.

lines.844: move data securely between application components, and that health requires more than
lines.845: secure transport. The additional properties the health sector requires — that exchanged data be
lines.846: clinically meaningful, structurally consistent, and governed by consent rules granular enough to
lines.847: reflect the sensitivity of individual health encounters — are not properties that the transport itself
lines.848: should supply. These are properties of the digital health systems that communicate, the shared
lines.849: specifications those systems conform to, and the governance arrangements around them —

lines.862: exchange substrate should therefore move and log health data faithfully without transforming or

unnumbered: Legend
• System (navy) — a participating system or component that sends or receives data.
• Access point (AP) — a participating organisation's own connection point in a distributed
model.
• Gateway — a component-specific interface that protects and mediates access to that
component.
• Service bus — shared infrastructure through which all traffic is routed.
• Event broker — shared infrastructure that distributes a published event to its subscribers.
• Solid line — exchange of data between endpoints.
• Dashed line — registration, logging and oversight, carrying no data content.
• Arrow — direction of event flow in the publish–subscribe model.
The exchange pattern a country adopts is an implementation choice. Direct connections link systems
point-to-point, conforming to open national specifications. A central service bus instead mediates all
traffic through a single shared channel. Gateways place a protective, mediating interface in front of
each component. In the distributed access-point model, each participating organisation (administrative
unit of participation) operates its own access point and a central authority provides registration, logging
and oversight without sitting in the path of the data itself. Publish–subscribe exchange is
asynchronous: a system publishes an event once, and any authorised subscriber receives it without

lines.4: The preceding chapters describe a reference architecture. This chapter addresses how
lines.5: countries move toward it: how to assess the starting point, sequence investment, specify the
lines.6: profiles that make the architecture implementable, verify conformance and progress, and put in
lines.7: place the people, skills, and financing that sustain it. It is written for the range of actors a
lines.8: national effort depends on — the ministries and agencies that govern it, the architects and
lines.9: modellers who design it, the implementers who build it, and the development partners who
lines.10: support it — and it is explicit, throughout, about who is accountable for each of these
lines.11: responsibilities.
lines.12: 4.1 Understanding the Starting Point
lines.13: 4.1.1 No Country Starts from Zero
lines.14: No country designing or implementing DPI-H begins from a blank slate. Every health system
lines.15: carries a legacy, including programme-specific applications built around particular funding
lines.16: priorities, national health information systems of varying capability, patient registries that sit in
lines.17: silos, and data still maintained in spreadsheets for reporting. The reference architecture, while
lines.18: ideal in outlook, recognises this legacy and aims to help countries understand which existing
lines.19: investments can be preserved, which should be upgraded to conform to open standards, which
lines.20: can be integrated into shared infrastructure, and which should be retired in favour of shared
lines.21: components that serve the whole system more efficiently.
lines.23: This chapter provides practical guidance for moving from the current state toward REDDHI —
lines.24: described in the preceding chapter not as a fixed destination to be reached and completed but
lines.25: as a continuously maturing direction of travel — through a structured, phased approach adapted
lines.26: to each country’s context, capability, and starting conditions.
lines.29: The most consequential investment a country can make before implementation begins is an
lines.30: honest assessment of its current digital health landscape. Countries that skip this step tend to
lines.31: build on unstable foundations — replicating fragmentation in new infrastructure, integrating with
lines.32: systems already scheduled for replacement, or investing in capabilities they already hold in
lines.34: A national digital health architecture assessment should answer four questions.

lines.35: What do we already have? Inventory all existing health information systems, registries, and
lines.36: digital tools, including those funded by development partners and individual programmes. For
lines.37: each, assess whether it performs a function that aligns with a REDDHI component, whether it is
lines.38: based on open standards, what population or geography it covers, and who owns and operates
lines.40: What is the state of our foundational DPI? Assess the reach and accessibility of national
lines.41: identity, payments, and data-exchange infrastructure. Understand which populations are
lines.42: covered, whether health use cases are legally and technically supported, and what integration
lines.43: mechanisms exist or need to be established.
lines.44: What are our governance and institutional conditions? Assess whether a legal and
lines.45: regulatory framework exists for health data, whether there is a designated institutional home for
lines.46: digital health architecture decisions, whether procurement mechanisms are aligned with open-
lines.47: standards requirements, and whether the capacity to design, implement, and sustain shared
lines.49: What are our priority health goals? Identify two to three high-value health goals — drawn
lines.50: from the seven priority goals that underpin this architecture — that have political support, a
lines.51: willing implementation community, and the potential to demonstrate tangible value quickly.
lines.52: Within each, identify the specific high-value use cases that will drive the first implementations.
lines.53: These goals, and the use cases within them, can anchor the initial implementation and provide
lines.54: the evidence base for broader investment.
lines.55: The outputs of this assessment form the foundation of a national digital health architecture
lines.56: roadmap: a living document that maps the current state, the target direction, the gap between
lines.57: them, and the sequenced investments required to close it. The roadmap is strengthened where
lines.58: it also sets out a benefits case and a simple logic model — connecting each investment to the
lines.59: capabilities it enables and the health outcomes it is expected to support — and where it draws
lines.60: on recognised digital-readiness and capability assessment frameworks, to establish a baseline
lines.61: against which progress can later be measured.
lines.65: Countries arrive at DPI-H implementation from different starting positions. Rather than
lines.66: prescribing a single implementation sequence, this guidance identifies four common entry points
lines.67: and describes how each advance toward REDDHI (Resilient Essential Data and Digital Health
lines.68: Infrastructure). Countries should identify which entry point most closely reflects their current
lines.69: reality and adapt the guidance accordingly.
lines.71: Entry point 1 — Building from the ground up.
lines.72: Countries with limited existing digital health infrastructure and early-stage foundational DPI face
lines.73: the challenge of establishing shared foundations from scratch. The risk here is that donor-

lines.74: funded projects move faster than national governance, creating new silos before shared
lines.75: infrastructure is in place. The priority for these countries is to establish governance and
lines.76: architectural standards before major technology investments are made, so that every
lines.77: subsequent investment conforms to a coherent national architecture rather than fragmenting it
lines.78: further. The REDDHI minimum viable layer then provides the sequenced starting point.
lines.79: Countries at this entry point should resist the pressure to deploy complex capabilities before the
lines.83: Countries with significant existing investment in programme-specific systems — disease-
lines.84: specific registries, immunisation systems, maternal and child health tools — face the challenge
lines.85: of connecting what they have without replacing it prematurely. The priority here is not
lines.86: replacement but integration: establishing the shared infrastructure layer alongside existing
lines.87: systems and progressively migrating functions as legacy systems reach end of life or require
lines.88: upgrade. For example, a client registry deployed as a shared identification layer, connected to
lines.89: existing systems through defined APIs, can immediately reduce duplication without disrupting
lines.90: ongoing programme delivery; and an interoperability capability that standardises data exchange
lines.91: between existing systems buys time for a more orderly transition to shared components.
lines.94: Countries that have already invested in shared health information infrastructure — but where
lines.95: those systems are not built on open standards, are not interoperable with foundational DPI, or
lines.96: are controlled by a single supplier — face a different challenge. The priority here is conformance
lines.97: and openness; assessing existing systems against open-standards requirements, negotiating
lines.98: with suppliers to expose standard APIs, and introducing governance frameworks that prevent
lines.99: future lock-in. Countries at this entry point should treat the right to move — the ability to replace,
lines.100: upgrade, or migrate to a different system in future — as a non-negotiable condition of any
lines.104: Countries with established shared infrastructure, strong governance, and advanced digital
lines.105: health capability face the challenge of deepening capability rather than establishing it: moving
lines.106: from foundational registries toward the business services layer, implementing semantic
lines.107: governance infrastructure, extending coverage to the last mile, and demonstrating the value of
lines.108: shared infrastructure through measurable health outcomes. The priority here is the sustainability
lines.109: of domestically financed national infrastructure, building the enterprise architecture capacity
lines.110: within government that can evolve the architecture over time, and engaging Ministries of
lines.111: Finance as strategic partners in the long-term financing of shared services.
lines.114: Regardless of entry point, implementation follows a broadly consistent phased progression. The
lines.115: phases are not strictly sequential — activities overlap and iterate — but they provide a practical
lines.116: structure for planning and sequencing investments, and the activities within each phase vary

lines.117: with a country's entry point. The indicative timeframes given below describe a typical sequence
lines.118: rather than a fixed schedule; actual durations depend heavily on starting conditions, governance
lines.119: readiness, and financing, and evaluation continues across all phases rather than only at the
lines.120: end. Several threads are not confined to a single phase but run throughout: governance,
lines.121: financing, partnership engagement, capacity development, and evaluation begin in Phase 1 and
lines.122: continue as the architecture matures. They appear below at the phase where they become most
lines.123: prominent, not the phase where they start.
lines.124: This phased approach is consistent with, and complements, the WHO Digital Implementation
lines.125: Investment Guide (DIIG),35 which sets out a step-by-step, needs-based process for planning
lines.126: and costing digital health interventions within a health programme. Where the DIIG guides the
lines.127: programme-level investment decision — from health need through costed implementation to
lines.128: monitoring — this guidance describes the shared infrastructure those investments align to and
lines.129: reuse, so that each programme deployment strengthens the national digital health enterprise
lines.130: rather than adding a parallel system.
lines.131: Phase 1 — Assess, align, and plan (indicative: the first few months).
lines.132: • Conduct the national architecture assessment described above, capturing baseline
lines.133: values for the outcomes the architecture is expected to influence.
lines.134: • Establish or strengthen the governance body responsible for digital health architecture
lines.136: • Engage stakeholders across health programmes, finance, identity, and ICT ministries.
lines.137: • Select two to three priority health goals, and the specific high-value use cases within
lines.138: them that will drive the first implementations and develop the business case and
lines.140: • Align procurement mechanisms with open-standards and conformance requirements.
lines.141: • Produce a national digital health architecture roadmap and an initial implementation
lines.142: plan, referring to recognised digital-readiness/ capability assessment frameworks.
lines.143: • Begin the financing and partnership conversation early — engaging Ministries of Finance
lines.144: and development partners around the business case, and setting the direction for

lines.226: 4.2.4 The Role of the National Digital Architect
lines.228: A recurring finding from country experience and global dialogue is that implementation fails not
lines.229: for lack of technology but for lack of someone accountable for the architecture as a whole. The

lines.230: Wilton Park dialogue on digital public infrastructure for health 36 identified the national digital
lines.231: architect — an individual or small team embedded in government, with the authority to define
lines.232: architectural standards, evaluate conformance, and enforce coordination across programmes
lines.233: and ministries — as one of the most urgent and actionable priorities for countries pursuing DPI-
lines.234: H. This role is not an IT manager, a project coordinator, or a donor-funded consultant. It is the
lines.235: accountable designer of the health system’s digital infrastructure — the person who holds the
lines.236: architectural blueprint, ensures every investment conforms to it, and has the authority to say no,
lines.237: or to escalate, when a proposed investment would undermine it.
lines.238: Because architectural coherence has to be maintained well beyond any single project, this
lines.239: should be established as an enduring function — part of business-as-usual governance —
lines.240: rather than a time-limited role, and put in place before major implementation begins, not after
lines.241: fragmentation has already set in, whether within the Ministry of Health, a dedicated digital health
lines.242: agency, or a whole-of-government digital authority. Countries need not face this in isolation:
lines.243: regional and global networks of national architects provide a means to share plans, compare
lines.244: approaches, and learn from one another’s experience. Progress along the path described here
lines.245: can then be tracked using the conformance and progress measures set out in section 4.4.

lines.600: recurrent cost, and for sustaining the case for continued investment.
lines.602: Partnerships extend well beyond financing. Sustainable DPI-H rests on relationships across
lines.603: government — with the authorities responsible for identity, payments, public financial
lines.604: management, and interoperability governance, many of which sit outside the health sector —
lines.605: and with regional bodies, standards organisations, and the wider implementer community.
lines.606: Development partners have a particular responsibility to align their contributions with the
lines.607: national architecture and roadmap rather than building parallel systems, and to express support
lines.608: in terms of the components and capabilities the country has prioritised. The national digital
lines.609: architect and the governance arrangements described earlier in this chapter are the means
lines.610: through which these relationships are coordinated in service of a coherent national architecture.

lines.3: Artificial intelligence and other emerging technologies are reshaping expectations of what digital
lines.4: health systems can achieve. Machine learning is being applied to diagnostic and decision support,
lines.5: risk prediction, image interpretation, the detection and forecasting of outbreaks, operational
lines.6: planning, and resource allocation. Large language and multi-modal models are changing how
lines.7: clinical knowledge is summarised, retrieved, and acted upon. Beyond these current applications,
lines.8: advances in AI agents, remote monitoring, wearable sensors, genomics, edge computing, and
lines.9: verifiable digital credentials each carry implications for how health data is generated, exchanged,
lines.10: and used. The pace of this change is unlikely to slow.
lines.11: This guidance does not attempt to catalogue emerging technologies or to predict their trajectories,
lines.12: both of which would date quickly. Its purpose is to set out the relationship between emerging
lines.13: technologies and the shared digital infrastructure described in this document, and to offer practical
lines.14: orientation for countries weighing where and how to adopt them. For artificial intelligence in
lines.15: particular, that orientation matters: implementers consistently report that the difficulty is less
lines.16: whether to adopt AI than knowing what, specifically, to adopt and on what foundations. General
lines.17: encouragement to adopt AI offers little to a ministry deciding where to invest.
lines.18: Artificial intelligence is understood here broadly, as machine-based systems that, for a given set
lines.19: of objectives, infer from the data they receive how to generate outputs such as predictions,
lines.20: recommendations, classifications, or decisions. This spans rule-based systems, statistical and
lines.21: machine learning models, and the large language and multi-modal models whose rapid public
lines.22: adoption from the early 2020s brought AI to the centre of health-sector attention. Several
lines.23: jurisdictions are now establishing legal definitions and governance frameworks for these
lines.24: systems42, and WHO has issued guidance on the ethics and governance of AI for health 43 and,
lines.25: more recently, on large multi-modal models specifically44.
lines.26: 5.1 Emerging technologies and the foundations they
lines.28: Emerging technologies do not substitute for the foundational work of building trusted registries,
lines.29: governed terminology, structured information models, and reliable interoperability. More often
lines.30: they depend on that work and integrate with it. Artificial intelligence, in particular, operates on top

lines.31: of existing digital infrastructure; where that infrastructure is weak, fragmented, or poorly governed,
lines.32: AI is less likely to perform as intended, with consequences for quality and patient safety.
lines.33: It is also relevant that not all emerging technologies draw on data held in the shared infrastructure.
lines.34: Some consumer-facing applications operate independently of health-system data, using
lines.35: information entered by individuals or collected through personal devices to offer self-management
lines.36: support or lifestyle advice, and these can deliver value without accessing shared records or
lines.37: interoperating with wider health information systems. The architecture described here concerns
lines.38: those technologies that depend on, or contribute to, the shared health data foundation, and it is
lines.39: for these that the relationship set out below is decisive.
lines.40: 5.2 Why data foundations determine what AI can
lines.42: The performance of an AI model depends on the data it can access, and in health that data is
lines.43: generated across many systems, providers, and points of care over a person's lifetime. Where
lines.44: data is fragmented, inconsistently coded, attributed to the wrong individual, or held in systems
lines.45: that do not exchange it, a model inherits and amplifies those weaknesses rather than overcoming
lines.46: them, and it does so at a scale and speed that can make the resulting errors difficult to detect and
lines.47: correct. A model used to identify patients at high risk of deterioration, for example, produces
lines.48: unreliable predictions if it draws only on records from a single facility while earlier admissions,
lines.49: laboratory results, and medication histories sit elsewhere and are not linked. The trusted data
lines.50: foundation that this architecture describes — captured once and reused many times — is what
lines.51: allows a model to be trained, validated, and deployed reliably, safely, and equitably.
lines.52: Several elements of the shared infrastructure are particularly important to the reliable
lines.53: performance of AI and other data-dependent technologies:
lines.54: • terminology services, which provide the semantic consistency that allows an algorithm to
lines.55: operate on data that means the same thing across the systems that produced it. Governed
lines.56: terminology also reduces the complexity a model has to contend with and improves the
lines.57: reliability with which it connects concepts;
lines.58: • the logical information model repository, which governs a shared, structured
lines.59: representation of data so that it is machine-processable rather than locked in free text or
lines.61: • the client registry, which enables the longitudinal records on which both training and
lines.62: inference depend to be assembled correctly for the right individual;
lines.63: • interoperability, a cross-cutting property realised through the information mediator and
lines.64: shared terminology rather than a component in its own right, which allows data to be linked
lines.65: across care settings and organisations, so that it can flow to where models are developed
lines.66: and recommendations can flow back to the point of care; and

lines.67: • the governance, consent, and privacy capabilities embedded throughout the architecture,
lines.68: which support the lawful and ethical use of data on which AI depends, and which retain
lines.69: public trust. Weaknesses in data quality cascade directly into the reliability of any
lines.70: analytical or AI capability built upon them.
lines.71: Two points deserve emphasis because they are easily overlooked. First, governance does not
lines.72: become less important as models become more capable; if anything it becomes more so. Large
lines.73: language and multi-modal models have well-documented limits in handling complex, inconsistent
lines.74: data, and consistent terminology and information models reduce that burden directly — making
lines.75: semantic governance an increasingly practical determinant of whether AI performs reliably, not
lines.76: only an ethical one. Second, grounding models in authoritative, governed reference data also
lines.77: bears on how far their outputs can be trusted. A model that draws on curated registries — a client
lines.78: registry, a facility registry, a terminology service, or a common geo-registry — rather than on
lines.79: ungoverned general-purpose sources can have its outputs traced back to source and audited
lines.80: before they inform a decision. Where an output would influence resource allocation, eligibility, or
lines.81: care, the discipline of auditing the data a model used, before acting on what it produced, is a
lines.82: meaningful safeguard. Models drawing only on ungoverned sources offer no comparable
lines.83: traceability, and an authoritative-looking answer is then hard to distinguish from an unfounded
lines.85: A related and rapidly developing pattern is to give models access to trusted, well-defined units of
lines.86: functionality rather than expecting the model to perform every task itself. Where a calculation
lines.87: should be identical everywhere — a coverage indicator, an eligibility rule, a conversion between
lines.88: units — it is more reliable to have the model call an authoritative service that performs that
lines.89: calculation deterministically than to have the model reproduce it, because the same input then
lines.90: yields the same result every time and the logic can be governed in one place. Emerging
lines.91: conventions describe these units in different ways:
lines.93: • as agents (components that orchestrate a task and that may in turn call a model, which
lines.95: • as shared interfaces — for example, servers implementing the Model Context Protocol
lines.96: (MCP) — through which a model can discover and invoke such capabilities.
lines.97: Designed well, this keeps models pointed at governed sources of truth for the parts of a task that
lines.98: need to be exact, while reserving the model's own inference for the parts that benefit from it. The
lines.99: registries, terminology services, and logical information model repository described in this
lines.100: guidance are what make such services trustworthy in the first place: a service that calculates an
lines.101: indicator is only authoritative if the records it draws on and the definition it applies — the
lines.102: numerator, denominator, and coded terms — are themselves governed.
lines.103: A related, forward-looking practice is to publish specifications and metadata in machine-readable
lines.104: form — for example, alongside published implementation guides — so that automated systems
lines.105: can discover and interpret the capabilities of a component reliably. As this practice matures it may
lines.106: become a useful readiness criterion for shared digital resources and metadata registries.

lines.107: 5.3 Where artificial intelligence can support the
lines.109: Across the priority health goals, the most credible near-term applications tend to be assistive
lines.110: rather than autonomous, and they fall broadly into two kinds: operational uses embedded in
lines.111: routine workflows, and analytical uses that support planning, monitoring, and decision-making.
lines.112: Illustrative examples, drawn from the domains examined in developing this architecture, include:
lines.113: • in health financing, support for claims adjudication and for the detection of fraud, waste,
lines.114: and abuse. It is useful to distinguish the two: detecting fraud relies on pattern analysis
lines.115: across large volumes of claims, whereas adjudication support concerns the evaluation of
lines.116: individual claims. Different techniques apply, from rule-based systems to machine
lines.117: learning, and current use of large language models in this area remains limited;
lines.118: • in the supply chain, demand forecasting, product classification and mapping to reference
lines.119: catalogues, quality control, and the detection of diversion or other anomalies;
lines.120: • in clinical services, diagnostic and decision support, image interpretation, risk prediction,
lines.121: and the detection and forecasting of outbreaks. These are functions of point-of-care
lines.122: clinical applications and analytical capabilities, supported by the shared foundation, rather
lines.123: than functions of any single shared component;
lines.124: • in planning and reach, estimating settlement patterns and population distribution from
lines.125: imagery to support microplanning and last-mile delivery. The limits here are instructive: a
lines.126: model may identify that a structure exists without determining its function, and a residential
lines.127: dwelling, a school, and an unoccupied structure carry very different implications for
lines.128: population estimates. Associated, governed reference data is what allows such a
lines.130: • across domains, extracting structured data from unstructured or scanned documents —
lines.131: for example, reading a scanned invoice, form, or report and converting it into coded,
lines.132: structured records that can be stored and reused — together with assistance in coding
lines.133: and in navigating complex guidance for different kinds of user.
lines.134: In each case, current good practice favours starting with assistive tools under human oversight
lines.135: rather than full automation, and combining automated analysis with human review at the points
lines.136: where consequences are significant. Framing adoption this way also helps decision-makers
lines.137: assess the broad benefit claims that frequently accompany AI offerings, by anchoring the question
lines.138: in a specific use case, the data it depends on, and the oversight it requires.

lines.142: AI readiness describes how well placed a country is to adopt AI safely, effectively, and
lines.143: sustainably; it is less a property of any particular model than of the environment into which a
lines.144: model would be introduced. It can be understood across three dimensions:
lines.145: • the quality and governance of the data a model would use;
lines.146: • the legal and policy framework governing its use; and
lines.147: • the institutional capacity to deploy, evaluate, monitor, and maintain it.
lines.148: Country-level legislation and organisational policies governing AI — covering data protection, the
lines.149: configuration of input and output safeguards, the quality and representativeness of training data,
lines.150: and the monitoring of model drift over time — are practical prerequisites for moving from pilots to
lines.151: routine use. WHO's guidance on the ethics and governance of AI for health 44, and its guidance
lines.152: on large multi-modal models45, set out principles and recommendations that countries can draw
lines.153: on, and several jurisdictions are establishing legal frameworks of their own.43,45,46,47
lines.154: 5.4.2 Trustworthy AI in a health setting
lines.155: Closely related to readiness is the question of what makes AI trustworthy in a health setting.
lines.156: Trustworthy AI is not a quality a product can assert for itself; it is earned through evidence that a
lines.157: system is effective for its stated purpose, safe, transparent about its limitations, accountable to
lines.158: identifiable people, fair across the populations it serves, and subject to meaningful human
lines.159: oversight. WHO's guidance on the ethics and governance of AI for health sets out consensus
lines.160: principles along these lines44, and its guidance on large multi-modal models extends them to
lines.161: generative systems45. A note of caution is warranted. Organisations are frequently approached
lines.162: with AI offerings that promise broad benefits, and this guidance is intended to help decision -
lines.163: makers interrogate such claims — asking what specific task a system performs, what data it
lines.164: depends on, how it was evaluated, who is accountable when it errs, and how its use is to be
lines.165: governed — rather than to encourage adoption for its own sake. More concretely, before a
lines.166: capability is relied upon, and at intervals thereafter, it should be evaluated against representative
lines.167: cases and explicit criteria, a discipline increasingly referred to as evaluation, or evals, so that its
lines.168: behaviour is understood and monitored rather than assumed. WHO maintains further resources
lines.169: on the responsible use of AI for health that countries can draw on 48.

lines.171: Equity and safety warrant particular attention. A model trained on data that is poorly governed or
lines.172: unrepresentative of the population it serves can reproduce and magnify existing inequities, and
lines.173: because it does so consistently and at scale, the effect can be harder to notice than an individual
lines.174: error. Attention to the representativeness and quality of the underlying data is therefore not a
lines.175: separate ethical exercise but part of the same data-foundation discipline on which performance
lines.178: Cost and sustainability are practical constraints rather than afterthoughts. Models differ markedly
lines.179: in the computing resources they require, pricing for commercial offerings can be volatile, and
lines.180: dependence on a single provider carries a risk of lock-in. Architectural choices that preserve the
lines.181: ability to substitute one model for another, and that separate the orchestration of a service from
lines.182: any particular model, reduce this exposure and keep options open as the technology and its
lines.183: economics evolve. Some countries are, in addition, exploring sovereign models — models hosted
lines.184: and governed within national or regional control — to keep sensitive data and critical capabilities
lines.185: under domestic authority; this can support data sovereignty and reduce dependence on a single
lines.186: external provider, though it carries its own cost and capacity implications.
lines.187: It is also worth being explicit about the commercial, economic, and political pressures that
lines.188: accompany emerging technologies. The visibility of AI can generate pressure — from vendors,
lines.189: donors, and political expectation — to invest in advanced capabilities before the foundations that
lines.190: make them viable are in place. A country that builds AI on fragmented foundations does not
lines.191: leapfrog the foundational work; it defers it at a higher eventual cost, and risks isolated pilots that
lines.192: perform well in controlled conditions but prove difficult to scale, generalise, or govern in routine
lines.193: practice. A more considered sequence — foundations first, capabilities as their value is
lines.194: demonstrated — tends to serve both better.
lines.195: 5.5 Keeping the architecture open and adaptable
lines.196: Building and maintaining the shared digital infrastructure for health is therefore itself central to
lines.197: preparing for emerging technologies. The same infrastructure that delivers value across the seven
lines.198: priority health goals is what makes AI and other innovations viable, safe, and sustainable. A
lines.199: country that has established trusted registries, governed semantics, and reliable interoperability
lines.200: is positioned to adopt new technologies as they mature, integrating them into a coherent
lines.201: ecosystem rather than attaching them to a fragmented one. The same principle applies to
lines.202: genomics, remote monitoring, and decentralised identity alike: the strength of the underlying
lines.203: infrastructure determines whether each new technology compounds the value of what already
lines.204: exists or simply adds another silo.
lines.205: The reference architecture is accordingly designed to remain open and adaptable. Flexibility at
lines.206: the interfaces between components, and in how those components are implemented, allows
lines.207: emerging technologies — including those not yet foreseeable — to be incorporated and scaled
lines.208: as they prove their worth, without the foundations having to be rebuilt. The foundations

lines.209: themselves, however, should not be regarded as static; they require ongoing stewardship,
lines.210: maintenance, and incremental evolution to sustain data quality, respond to changing needs, and
lines.211: absorb new technologies as they emerge.
lines.212: The definition of digital public infrastructure is itself evolving, and it is plausible that capabilities
lines.213: now treated as supporting technologies, including aspects of AI, may in time be recognised as
lines.214: reusable shared components in their own right. For the present, the architecture treats AI as a
lines.215: cross-cutting consideration rather than a defined component or a single platform, reflecting both
lines.216: how quickly the field is moving and the fact that analytical needs differ across health goals. The
lines.217: architecture remains open to revisiting that position as the technology and the surrounding
lines.219: Countries are therefore encouraged to view AI and other emerging technologies not as an
lines.220: alternative to the foundational investments described in this guidance, but as a compelling
lines.221: reason to make and sustain them. Strong digital and data foundations are what allow health
lines.222: systems to meet current needs while adopting new technologies safely, effectively, and at scale,
lines.223: both now and as the field continues to change.

lines.48: The Client Registry is the national authoritative source of health-specific person identity. It is the
lines.49: foundational health-sector component that maintains a unique, verifiable identity record for every person
lines.50: who accesses health services and provides the identity resolution services that allow other systems to
lines.51: consistently identify that same person across the fragmented landscape of health information systems. It
lines.52: holds the minimum set of demographic attributes needed to uniquely identify a person, assigns and
lines.53: manages health-specific unique identifiers, links multiple local or system-specific identifiers to a single
lines.54: person record, and resolves ambiguous matches through deduplication and probabilistic matching.
lines.55: The Client Registry is not a clinical record. It holds identity data — who a person is — not health data that
lines.56: describes what has happened to them. Its purpose is to ensure that every other system that records, stores,
lines.57: or exchanges health data about a person can be certain it is referring to the same individual. Without that
lines.58: assurance, person-centred care, longitudinal health records, and cross-programme data aggregation
lines.59: cannot be achieved with the reliability or integrity that health system decision-making requires.
lines.60: In the DPI-H reference architecture, the Client Registry may also be described as a Master Patient Index
lines.61: (MPI) or Enterprise Master Patient Index (EMPI), particularly in contexts where the scope spans multiple
lines.62: health care organisations or information systems. The term 'Client Registry' is used here in preference to
lines.63: 'patient registry' to reflect the broad range of interactions a person has with the health system — as a
lines.64: patient, a carer, a health service user, or a community member — none of which are fully captured by the
lines.68: Person-centred care depends on knowing who the person is. A clinician ordering a test, dispensing a
lines.69: medicine, or reviewing a referral needs confidence that the record they are looking at belongs to the person
lines.70: in front of them — not a near-duplicate created by a different facility, a name variant, or a data entry error.
lines.71: When that confidence is absent, the integrity of every clinical decision that depends on it is at risk. At scale,
lines.72: fragmented identity produces fragmented data: disease surveillance is unreliable, population health
lines.73: indicators are inflated by duplicates, and programme performance cannot be measured with integrity.
lines.74: The stakes are higher for vulnerable populations. People who access services under different names —
lines.75: due to stigma, discrimination, or transient living circumstances — are especially susceptible to identity
lines.76: fragmentation. Migrants and refugees without foundational identification documents risk being invisible to
lines.77: the health system entirely. Children born outside formal registration systems may be denied services. A

lines.126: the authoritative source for a person's legal identity: name, date of birth, sex, and nationality. They are not

lines.128: Functional health ID systems, including the Health Unique Identifier (HUID), are created to manage
lines.129: identification for the specific use cases of health service delivery. They may or may not be linked to
lines.130: foundational ID, depending on a country's context. The WHO HUID Guidance (2023) identifies three primary
lines.131: implementation models that countries have adopted:
lines.132: – Model A — HUID linked to national ID or CRVS. Where a robust foundational ID system exists,
lines.133: the HUID is derived from or permanently linked to the foundational identifier. The Client Registry
lines.134: stores the linkage and uses the foundational ID as the primary identity proofing source. This
lines.135: reduces duplication and strengthens the accuracy of identity resolution.
lines.136: – Model B — HUID not linked to national ID. Where a foundational ID system is absent, unreliable,
lines.137: or inaccessible to the health sector, the health system creates its own functional identifier
lines.138: independently. The Client Registry is the authoritative source for this health-specific identifier and
lines.139: manages its own identity proofing processes.
lines.140: – Model C — Multiple local health IDs linked through an EMPI. Where multiple facilities or
lines.141: programmes have each assigned their own local identifiers to the same population, the Client
lines.142: Registry functions as an Enterprise Master Patient Index — maintaining a cross-reference map
lines.143: that links these local identifiers to a single canonical person record.
lines.144: In all three models, the Client Registry does not duplicate foundational ID data or attempt to replicate civil
lines.145: registration. Where a foundational ID exists, the Client Registry stores the identifier as a reference attribute
lines.146: and may query the foundational system to verify identity at registration; it does not absorb or maintain the
lines.147: authoritative record. Where foundational ID is absent, the Client Registry is the health sector's fallback, not
lines.149: Countries should be aware that linking a health identifier to a national ID or social protection registry creates
lines.150: both opportunities and risks. The opportunity is stronger identity assurance and more accurate cross-

Governance of the Client Registry follows the cross-cutting governance framework in
Section 3.4 of the guidance document. Component-specific considerations include:
(1) The Client Registry sits at the intersection of health, civil registration, social
protection, and potentially financial services. Its governance should be explicitly multi-
sectoral: a single Ministry of Health cannot unilaterally govern a component whose
data is referenced across government. A formal governance body with mandated
participation from health, civil registration, and data protection authorities is required.
(2) The decision of whether to link the HUID to a foundational identifier — and to which
one — is a policy decision with significant privacy, equity, and institutional
GOVERNANCE
implications. This decision should be taken at the highest appropriate level of
government, supported by a privacy impact assessment and a legal framework,
before technical implementation proceeds.
(3) The right to be registered should be universal. Governance should ensure that
absence of foundational documentation never becomes grounds for denial of health
identity or service access.
(4) Merge and link decisions that affect a person's health record should be reviewable
by the person themselves where technically and legally feasible, consistent with data
subject rights under applicable frameworks.

lines.7: The Health Facility Registry is the national authoritative source of identity, location, and classification data
lines.8: for all facilities, locations, and organisations through which health services are delivered or that are of direct
lines.9: relevance to the Ministry of Health’s mandate. This scope is intentionally broader than a list of permanent
lines.10: clinical facilities. It encompasses: permanent clinical facilities such as hospitals, health centres, clinics,
lines.11: pharmacies, and laboratories; logistics facilities such as warehouses and distribution centres; community
lines.12: health posts and outreach sites; temporary and campaign facilities such as vaccination posts, emergency
lines.13: field hospitals, and mobile clinics established for specific programmes or emergencies; and, where
lines.14: nationally defined, other locations whose activities intersect with public health responsibilities. The registry
lines.15: covers facilities across all sectors: public, private, faith-based, and NGO. A single standardised, uniquely
lines.16: identified, and centrally governed record is maintained for each facility, providing the common reference
lines.17: against which clinical, financial, logistical, and administrative systems can consistently identify and locate
lines.18: the places where health services are delivered.
lines.19: The registry and the Master Facility List are closely related but architecturally distinct. The Health Facility
lines.20: Registry is the system — the technology, governance processes, and workflows that collect, validate,
lines.21: maintain, and publish facility data. The Master Facility List (MFL) is the output of that system: the
lines.22: standardised, uniquely coded list of all active facilities that the registry produces and keeps current. A
lines.23: country may have an MFL without having a formal Health Facility Registry; the DPI-H reference architecture
lines.24: calls for the registry infrastructure that makes the MFL reliable, interoperable, and sustainably maintained.
lines.25: An important architectural principle underlies the design of the Health Facility Registry: facilities, buildings,
lines.26: locations, and organisations are distinct entities that should not be conflated. A facility is a defined health
lines.27: service delivery unit — it has a scope of services, an operator, and a governance status. A building is a
lines.28: physical structure: a facility may operate across multiple buildings, or multiple facilities may share one
lines.29: building. A location is a geographic reference: a facility may have a primary location and satellite locations
lines.30: or move entirely. An organisation is the legal entity that operates the facility. Keeping these distinctions
lines.31: clear matters for practical registry design. A facility that relocates to a new building retains its identity and
lines.32: service history. A temporary vaccination post is a distinct facility record with its own lifecycle, linked to the
lines.33: organising entity but not absorbed into a permanent facility’s record. An organisation that operates multiple
lines.34: facilities appears in a separate organisational register but is linked to many facility records. These
lines.35: distinctions also underpin the principle of referential integrity: each entity should be managed in one
lines.36: authoritative place and referenced everywhere else, not duplicated across systems.

unnumbered: The Health Facility Registry is a core DPI-H foundational component — the national
authoritative source of identity, location, and classification data for health facilities.
It is closely related to two other concepts that warrants distinction. The Master
Facility List (MFL) is the standardised dataset that the Health Facility Registry
ARCHITECTURE
produces and governs — the registry is the technology; the MFL is the data. The
PLACEMENT
Common Geo-Registry (CGR) is a cross-sectoral foundational component that
AND KEY
manages geographic objects (administrative units, settlements, boundaries) with
DISTINCTION
temporal integrity. The Health Facility Registry would depend on a CGR (where it
exists) for its geographic reference data but is not the same thing: the CGR governs
geography; the Health Facility Registry governs health facilities positioned within
that geography.
1 WHAT IT IS

lines.37: The geographic dimension of the Health Facility Registry deserves particular attention. Facilities exist at
lines.38: specific geographic locations within administrative and reporting hierarchies that change over time —
lines.39: districts split, boundaries are redrawn, new administrative levels are created. A Health Facility Registry that
lines.40: treats geographic location as a static attribute quickly becomes unreliable for aggregate reporting,
lines.41: particularly when data from different periods needs to be compared across changing administrative
lines.42: boundaries. Managing this temporal dimension — knowing not just where a facility is now but which
lines.43: administrative unit it belonged to on a given date — is one of the most technically and institutionally
lines.44: demanding aspects of facility data governance.
lines.47: Effective health service delivery, financing, and planning all depend on knowing where health facilities are,
lines.48: what they do, and whether they are operational. Without a reliable, interoperable health facility registry,
lines.49: every system in the health ecosystem maintains its own local version of the facility list — and those lists
lines.50: may diverge. For example, a logistics management system may route supplies to facilities that may not
lines.51: always match to the claims system's provider identifiers; there may be difficulty in attributing a case report
lines.52: to the correct administrative unit because its facility list references a district that was divided in a prior
lines.53: period; and health system managers may face challenges with reimbursing services at facilities whose
lines.54: operational status have not been updated since the last manual audit.
lines.55: These examples reflect conditions of health systems that lack a governed health facility registry. The
lines.56: consequences, not merely administrative inconvenience, result in reduced ability to allocate resources
lines.57: equitably, reduced visibility of where the health system is and is not functioning, and reduced capacity to
lines.58: respond to health emergencies. During the COVID-19 pandemic, the absence of geolocated, current facility
lines.59: data in many countries made it materially harder to plan vaccine delivery, identify capacity gaps, and route
lines.60: supplies. This gap was a key motivation for the WHO Geolocated Health Facilities Data initiative, which
lines.61: notes that the pandemic exposed urgent gaps in countries’ ability to locate health facilities, impeding
lines.62: equitable access to diagnostics, therapeutics, and vaccines (WHO, Geolocated Health Facilities Data
lines.64: When a Health Facility Registry is in place, current and maintained, the entire health information
lines.65: infrastructure gains a stable geographic anchor with benefits to health service users and health systems
lines.66: stakeholders alike; and while it does not deliver these outcomes directly, it provides the stable reference
lines.67: on which they become possible. For example:
lines.68: • Accurate attribution of health workers to their deployed facilities, supporting workforce planning and
lines.70: • Routing and delivery of health products and commodities to verified locations.
lines.71: • Validation of health coverage scheme claims against known, empanelled providers.
lines.72: • Modelling of service coverage by planners against population distribution.
lines.73: • Aggregation of case data across administrative hierarchies for public health surveillance, with
lines.74: confidence that the boundaries used are consistent over time.

Governance of the Health Facility Registry follows the cross-cutting governance
framework in Section 3.4 of the guidance document. Component-specific
considerations include:
(1) The Health Facility Registry typically has multiple institutional data contributors —
Ministries of Health, subnational health administrations, professional councils, and
faith-based and NGO facility networks — each with legitimate authority over different
subsets of facility data. The governance framework should clearly define which
institution is the steward for each facility type, what verification is required before a
new facility can be published, and what approval is needed before a closure is
recorded. Faith-based and private sector facility data is a particular challenge in many
countries. In several sub-Saharan African and South Asian countries, a substantial
proportion of health services — in some cases exceeding 30% of total service delivery
— is provided by faith-based or private sector facilities that maintain their own
administrative hierarchies (WHO/USAID MFL Resource Package, 2019). A national
Health Facility Registry that covers only public sector facilities would not fulfil its full
GOVERNANCE
function.
(2) Hierarchy changes require coordinated cross-institutional governance. When a
district is divided, every system that aggregates data by district — surveillance, HMIS,
supply chain — is affected. The governance framework should specify who has
authority to update hierarchy linkages, what notification is required before a change
is implemented, and what retrospective recalculation obligations apply for historical
indicators.
(3) The distinction between provenance and ownership of facility data should be
defined. A facility may be owned by a faith-based organisation but listed in a national
public registry; the data custodian (the Ministry of Health) and the data owner (the
facility operator) have different governance roles and rights. The governance
framework should address this explicitly.
(4) The Health Facility Registry should be designed as a public good: facility identity
and location data, at minimum, should be publicly accessible in alignment with the
WHO GHFD initiative's open data objectives and the principle that patients and
communities have a right to know where health services are available.

lines.226: Core Registries for Health · DPI-H Foundational Layer
lines.230: The Health Workforce Registry is the national authoritative record of identity, credential, and classification
lines.231: data for all health workers recognised as part of the national health workforce — including licensed or
lines.232: certified professionals employed in both public and private sectors and, where nationally defined and
lines.233: registered, community health workers and other cadres operating in informal or semi-formal capacities. It
lines.234: maintains a standardised, uniquely identified record for each health worker, providing the common
lines.235: reference point against which clinical, administrative, financing, and regulatory systems can consistently
lines.236: identify, verify, and classify the people delivering health services.
lines.237: The registry holds two interlocking categories of information:
lines.238: 1. The first is identity: who the health worker is — their demographics, unique identifier, and may
lines.240: 2. The second is credentials: what the health worker is qualified and authorised to do — their
lines.241: occupational classification, professional registration, licensing status, and qualifications.
lines.242: Together, these form the data foundation for a health system that can assure the quality and accountability
lines.244: The WHO National Health Workforce Accounts (NHWA) handbook (Second Edition, 2023) defines 29
lines.245: indicators that underpin health workforce monitoring, planning, and policy — covering stock, flow,
lines.246: education, migration, and expenditure. The national health workforce registry is a key data source for 12 of
lines.247: these indicators, notably those measuring stock and flow – critical to workforce planning and equitable
lines.248: distribution. The Health Workforce Registry, as defined in the DPI-H reference architecture, provides the
lines.249: foundational data infrastructure from which these indicators can be derived.
lines.252: Health systems deliver care through people. The quality, safety, and equity of that care depend on knowing
lines.253: who those people are, what they are qualified to do, and where they are deployed. Ministries of Health need
lines.254: to determine whether a health worker is legitimately registered, where workforce shortages are emerging,
lines.255: or whether payroll rolls include inactive or unqualified personnel. Without a reliable national registry, health
lines.256: worker data can be fragmented across professional councils, employer HR systems, facility registers, and
lines.257: paper-based records and these can sometimes be inconsistent, incomplete, and may not always be current.

unnumbered: The Health Workforce Registry is a core DPI-H foundational component — the
shared identity and credential anchor for health workers across the health
ecosystem. It is architecturally distinct from two operational systems: the Human
Resources Information System (HRIS), which manages employment transactions,
ARCHITECTURE
payroll processing, leave management, and workforce scheduling; and the Learning
PLACEMENT
Management System (LMS), which manages training delivery, course enrolment,
and assessment. The Health Workforce Registry holds the authoritative master
record of who a health worker is and what they are qualified and licensed to do. The
HRIS and LMS consume this registry as their reference source; neither replaces it.

lines.305: The Health Workforce Registry is one of the Core Registries for Health within the DPI-H reference
lines.306: architecture. Its closest structural counterpart is the Client Registry with each providing a shared identity
lines.307: anchor — one for health service users, the other for health workers. Both follow similar patterns of unique
lines.308: identifier management, multi-identifier cross-referencing, and standards-based query APIs.
lines.309: The Health Facility Registry is the Health Workforce Registry's primary peer dependency. A health worker
lines.310: record without a facility affiliation has limited operational value; a facility record without linked workforce
lines.311: data cannot support staffing analysis. The two registries are designed to be jointly queried — through the
lines.312: IHE Mobile Care Services Discovery (mCSD) profile, which covers both health worker and facility data —
lines.313: to answer questions about workforce distribution, service availability, and facility capacity.
lines.314: The Terminology Service can host the standardised occupation codes, qualification categories, and
lines.315: specialisation taxonomies that give health worker classification data its semantic meaning. Without
lines.316: consistent coding anchored in a Terminology Service, it may prove difficult to reliably aggregate workforce
lines.317: data from different sources. The Logical Information Model Repository holds the canonical schema defining
lines.318: what attributes a health worker record should contain, their cardinalities, and their terminology bindings.

lines.327: • Health workforce planning and analytics systems can draw on it to produce supply-side workforce
lines.329: • Learning management systems can reference it to track CPD completion and update qualification

Governance of the Health Workforce Registry follows the cross-cutting governance
framework in Section 3.4 of the guidance document. Component-specific
considerations include:
(1) The Health Workforce Registry has a structurally complex multi-institutional
governance context. Professional licensing authorities, Ministries of Health, employer
HR systems, training institutions, and subnational health administrations are all
authoritative sources for different attributes of a health worker record. The governance
framework should specify which institution is the steward for each attribute type, and
what verification is required before an attribute can be published.
GOVERNANCE (2) Licence status data has direct patient safety implications: a system that publishes
an incorrect licence status — particularly one that shows a revoked licence as active
— can contribute to a patient safety incident. Governance should therefore specify
the maximum permissible latency between a licensing authority revoking a licence
and that change being reflected in the registry, and should define the incident
response process for discovered discrepancies.
(3) Health workers have a direct personal interest in their own registry record — their
ability to practise depends on it. Governance should provide a defined process for
health workers to review their own record, raise disputes, and have errors corrected
within a specified timeframe.
(4) For community health workers and cadres without formal professional regulation,
the governance framework should specify which institution is responsible for
maintaining their registry records, how their identity is verified at registration, and what
attributes are required.

unnumbered: The Product Registry is a foundational DPI-H component holding core product
master data — standardised, and cross-sectorally reusable. It is architecturally
distinct from the Product Catalogue Management tool, which extends the registry
with richer, operationally enriched attributes specific to health supply chain use

lines.7: The Lifelong Health Record (LHR) is one or more governed data repositories, whether physically
lines.8: consolidated or virtually federated, that collectively maintain a longitudinal, person-centred record of an
lines.9: individual's health and healthcare-related data in computable, standards-based format. It aggregates
lines.10: clinical data contributed from multiple source systems — including facility-based care, community health
lines.11: programmes, laboratories, pharmacies, and, where applicable, individuals themselves — into a coherent
lines.12: view that no single source system produces independently. It makes that view securely accessible to
lines.13: authorised health workers, systems, and individuals in accordance with the person's consent preferences
lines.14: and the applicable legal framework.
lines.15: The LHR is defined by its outcome, not by its implementation model. A centralised national health record,
lines.16: a federated architecture in which data remains at source and is assembled on demand, a hybrid approach,
lines.17: or a virtual record assembled through standardised query interfaces are all valid expressions of the LHR
lines.18: capability. What matters is that the outcome is achieved: a person's clinically relevant health information is
lines.19: governed, longitudinal, accessible to authorised actors when and where it is needed, and under the
lines.20: meaningful control of the individual to whom it belongs. As a foundational shared data component, the LHR
lines.21: is not an optional enrichment to the architecture — it is part of the minimum viable foundation. Without it,
lines.22: the continuity of care, clinical decision support, and person-centred capabilities that the DPI-H architecture
lines.23: is designed to enable cannot be delivered. The reference architecture defines the outcomes the LHR should
lines.24: achieve and the requirements any compliant implementation needs to satisfy, without constraining the
lines.25: architectural choices through which countries achieve them.
lines.26: The LHR is not a massive central data lake of every clinical fact ever generated by every system. It is a
lines.27: curated longitudinal view of a person's clinically relevant data — sufficient to support continuity of care
lines.28: across providers, but not intended to duplicate every source system's operational workload. Source
lines.29: systems retain their operational data; the LHR holds the governed, shared, person-attributed view that
lines.30: crosses institutional and system boundaries. This distinction has significant implications for what countries
lines.31: need to build, how data flows are governed, and what consuming applications can reasonably expect to

unnumbered: The Lifelong Health Record (LHR) is the term used in this reference architecture in
preference to the Shared Health Record (SHR) — the term used in the OpenHIE
architecture specification — to reflect the longitudinal, person-centred nature of the
capability: a record that spans a person's entire life and all their interactions with the
TERMINOLOGY health system, regardless of where or how it is implemented. In the DPI-H reference

ARCHITECTURE metadata registries for health, the Terminology Service, and the LIMR. Together

health system to deliver digitally-enabled care. The LHR is the governed, person-
centred DPI-H component that aggregates clinical and health-related data across
those systems and makes it longitudinally available.
